sens: To be well received, to find favor with God
To please God through one's actions and way of life
To satisfy God, to be approved by Him
G2100.detail:
1. The word describes a relationship where something or someone pleases God, where God receives it favorably. It is the image of an offering or a conduct that finds grace in the eyes of God. Enoch had this relationship: "he had this testimony that he pleased God" (Hebrews 11:5), which means that his entire life was accepted and approved by God.

2. This is particularly manifested through faith and the way of living: "without faith it is impossible to please Him" (Hebrews 11:6), which shows that it is a matter of trust and obedience, not appearances. Faith is the condition for our entire life to be pleasing to God.

3. Acts of generosity and service towards others please God: "it is with such sacrifices that God is pleased" (Hebrews 13:16). This refers to charity, sharing, concrete actions that reflect the love of God.
G2100.origine: The word comes from the Greek "eu" (good) and "aresteō" (to be suitable, to please, to arrange). The basic image is that of something that "fits well" with someone, that is suitable for them. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this word often translates "hiler" (to walk with God, to be pleasing), notably for Enoch who "walked with God": the idea is one of harmonious communion, a life that pleases the one with whom one walks.
G2100.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the Epistle to the Hebrews. In each case, it concerns the relationship of humans with God — not the reverse. It first describes Enoch, a man who was "pleasing to God" before his miraculous removal (Hebrews 11:5). The epistle then establishes that this is impossible without faith (Hebrews 11:6), emphasizing that this pleasingness is not a matter of human performance but of trust in God. Finally, the epistle applies this word to concrete acts of generosity and service: these sacrifices, these gestures of sharing, are those that please God (Hebrews 13:16). The word thus designates a relationship that is expressed by faith on one hand, and by acts of charity on the other.
G2100.portee: This word reminds the believer that their life can please God — not through merit or perfection, but through faith. Like Enoch, everyone can walk with God by trusting Him. It also shows that concrete acts of generosity and sharing are not detached from faith: they are sacrifices that directly please God, visible expressions of faith that honor Him.

sens: that pleases, that satisfies
that is accepted with favor
that is suitable, that is appropriate
that deserves approval
G2101.detail:
1. In the simplest sense, pleasing describes what pleases someone, what brings them joy. Paul urges the Romans to offer their bodies "as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God" (Romans 12:1): the image is that of a gift that pleases the one who receives it.

2. The word also expresses the idea of being accepted with favor, of obtaining approval. The one who serves Christ "is pleasing to God and approved by men" (Romans 14:18): it is an acceptance, a positive recognition.

3. Pleasing can mean "in accordance with the will", "that fits". Believers must "discern what is the will of God, what is good, pleasing, and perfect" (Romans 12:2): pleasing qualifies here what aligns with God's plan.

4. The word is also used for what personally pleases God as judge and master. Paul tells servants to be "pleasing" to their masters (Titus 2:9) and children to obey their parents "in all things, for this is pleasing to the Lord" (Colossians 3:20): obedience and faithfulness are pleasing.
G2101.origine: The word comes from two roots: "eu" (good) and "arestos" (that satisfies, that fits). The starting image is that of what "goes well", what adapts perfectly. In classical Greek, the word designates what pleases or fits. The Bible uses it to express not only personal satisfaction but also conformity to God's will and divine acceptance.
G2101.emploi: The word appears nine times in the New Testament, concentrated in the Pauline epistles (Romans, Corinthians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, Titus) and Hebrews. Paul mainly uses it to describe what pleases God: how to live to be pleasing to Him (2 Corinthians 5:9), how to discern His will (Romans 12:2), how to serve with a heart that pleases the Lord. The word also extends to human relationships: obeying masters, parents. It is a key term for Christian ethics: showing that one's life, choices, and actions please God.
G2101.portee: For the Christian, this word invites a complete rethinking of life as a "pleasing sacrifice" to God (Romans 12:1) — not out of fear or servile obligation, but out of grateful love. It is a profound orientation: examining one's actions, words, and obedience by asking whether they truly please the Lord. This even transforms the work of the servant or the obedience of the child into an act of worship.

sens: in a way that pleases God, that satisfies Him
with divine acceptance and favor
G2102.detail:
1. This word describes a manner of acting or living that pleases God, that obtains His approval. In Hebrews 12:28, Paul exhorts believers to serve God "in a pleasing manner" — that is, with worship and recognition that truly satisfies Him.
2. The idea is one of happy acceptance by God: when one does something "in a pleasing manner", one does not merely accomplish it, one does it in such a way that God finds pleasure and satisfaction in it.
G2102.origine: The word comes from the Greek "eu" (good) and "arestos" (pleasing, that fits). It is the adverb formed from the adjective "arestos", which literally means "that adjusts to, that fits". The root evokes the idea of "adapting to" or "corresponding to", hence the meaning of "pleasing to" or "acceptable to".
G2102.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 12:28. Paul uses it to express how believers should offer their worship and recognition to God now that they have received an unshakeable kingdom. It is a call to serve God not out of obligation or habit, but in a way that is truly acceptable in His eyes — with sincerity, reverence, and gratitude.
G2102.portee: This word reminds the Christian that God is not satisfied with empty or mechanical religious acts; He demands worship, obedience, and recognition that are truly pleasing to Him. It is an invitation to examine one's motivations: does our worship truly please God, or do we do it out of tradition or fear? It pushes us to cultivate a sincere relationship with Him.

sens: Christian from Rome mentioned in Paul's letter to Timothy
G2103.detail: Eubulus is a believer who lived in Rome at the time Paul was writing his second letter to Timothy. His name literally means "one who deliberates well" (eu = well, boule = counsel). He is among the disciples who send their greetings to Timothy, alongside Pudens, Linus, and Claudia, indicating that he was known and respected in the Roman Christian community of that time.
G2103.origine: The name Eubulus comes from ancient Greek and means "one who has good counsel" or "who deliberates well," composed of eu (well) and boule (counsel, deliberation). It is a Greek name borne by notable figures in the ancient world, but only this Eubulus is known as a disciple of Christ.
G2103.emploi: Eubulus appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 4:21, in Paul's final words. The context shows that Paul, imprisoned in Rome and knowing his end is near, lists the names of those who remain faithful and greet Timothy. The mention of Eubulus alongside Pudens, Linus (who would later become a leader of the Church of Rome), and Claudia suggests that he was an established and trusted Christian in the Roman community, capable of supporting the work of the Gospel in difficult times.
G2103.portee: Eubulus's presence in this passage shows that the early Church relied on faithful believers whose names remain unknown to us beyond these simple mentions. His example reminds us that most servants of God remain in anonymity, but their faithfulness in trials (like that which Paul experienced in prison) is precious and worthy of remembrance.

sens: Who comes from a high-ranking family, of elevated status
Who manifests greatness of soul, moral rectitude
G2104.detail:
1. The word primarily designates someone of high birth, belonging to an aristocratic or royal family. In Luke 19:12, the man in the parable is described as 'eugénès' — he is of noble birth, hence his status as a future king. It is the notability of lineage and social rank.
2. By extension, it characterizes a moral quality: a noble soul, capable of discernment and integrity. In Acts 17:11, the Jews of Berea have 'noble sentiments' (literally: a noble soul, eugénès): they do not receive the word blindly, but examine it seriously. This kind of nobility is not of blood, but of spirit.
G2104.origine: The Greek word combines εὖ ('well') and γένος ('race, birth, lineage'). It evokes the idea of a well-placed birth, an honorable origin. The root γένος is found in French in 'généalogie' and 'genre'. In Hebrew, the Septuagint sometimes translates גָּדוֹל ('great') with this word, showing that the greatness of birth and moral greatness are often linked in biblical thought.
G2104.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament with two distinct nuances. In Luke 19:12 and 1 Corinthians 1:26, it describes the social status of birth — a person of elevated condition, people of noble rank. In Acts 17:11, it shifts to the moral sense: the Bereans are 'noble' not by their lineage, but by their disposition to listen to the Word with discernment. Paul also uses it in the comparative in Acts 17:11. This transition from the concrete (birth) to the figurative (moral quality) is characteristic of the moral vocabulary of the New Testament.
G2104.portee: This word reminds us of a central truth of the Gospel: true nobility is not of blood or social rank, but of the heart. The Bereans are praised not because they are of high lineage, but because they receive the Word with uprightness and vigilance. For the Christian, it is an invitation to seek moral greatness — honesty, discernment, receptivity to truth — rather than worldly honors.

sens: Weather condition characterized by a clear and open sky, without clouds or storms
G2105.detail: 1. The word designates good weather, this atmospheric condition that everyone recognizes: a clear, bright sky, conducive to outdoor activities. In Matthew 16:2, Jesus cites this popular saying that people utter when seeing a red sky in the evening: they conclude that it will be nice the next day. It is the simplest and most common weather observation.
G2105.origine: The Greek word comes from the adjective 'eudios' which literally means 'under a good sky' or 'under a favorable sky' (eu- = good, dios = sky, from Zeus). It is a natural compound to express the idea of a serene and clear atmosphere. The word rarely appears in ancient texts, making it a rather specialized and local expression.
G2105.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: in Matthew 16:2, where Jesus criticizes those who know how to interpret the signs of the sky to predict the weather, but who cannot discern the signs of the present times. The context is not a lesson in meteorology, but a lesson on spiritual blindness: people are attentive to small earthly signs but blind to the great signs of God.
G2105.portee: This passage invites the reader to reflect on their priorities: do we have the same zeal to observe spiritual signs as people do to predict rain or good weather? Jesus urges us to cultivate a moral and spiritual insight that transcends the observation of the visible world.

sens: To give one's consent to something, to judge that it is good
To take pleasure in someone or something, to rejoice in it
To manifest satisfaction towards a person, to fully approve them
G2106.detail:
1. The verb primarily means 'to judge good' or 'to consent to': it is to freely decide that something is good and to adhere to it. In Luke 12:32, the Father consents to give the kingdom to His disciples — He judges it good and does so willingly. In Romans 15:27, the churches of Asia have voluntarily decided to contribute to the needs of the saints in Jerusalem.
2. It also means 'to take pleasure' or 'to find joy' in something or someone. The verb carries the idea of personal satisfaction, a sincere approval that comes from the heart. In 2 Thessalonians 2:12, the unbelievers take pleasure in injustice — they rejoice in it.
3. Applied to God, it manifests His absolute approval towards someone. At the three decisive moments of Jesus' ministry — His baptism (Matthew 3:17), the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:5), and the heavenly Voice of the Father (2 Peter 1:17) — God declares: 'in you I have placed all my affection'; He fully approves Jesus and bestows upon Him His benevolent favor.
G2106.origine: The Greek word is formed from εὖ ('well') and δοκέω ('to judge, to believe'), hence the literal meaning: 'to judge well'. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew verb רָצָה ('to be pleased, to approve'), particularly when God accepts an offering or approves someone. This common root ('benevolent judgment') connects the word to the idea of a decision that is not forced, but free and joyful.
G2106.emploi: The verb appears 21 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul. It is first used with an infinitive: to consent to do something (Romans 15:26-27, Galatians 1:15). It is also used with the dative ('to be pleased with', 2 Thessalonians 2:12) or with ἐν ('to be pleased in', Matthew 3:17; Mark 1:11). Applied to God the Father, it denotes His contentment with Jesus and His free and sovereign will (Colossians 1:19, 1 Corinthians 1:21). Applied to humans, it means to consent, to prefer, or to rejoice in something (2 Corinthians 5:8: Paul prefers to be away from the body).
G2106.portee: This word reveals that divine satisfaction towards Jesus and His people is not a distant judgment, but a deep and personal approval. Knowing that the Father has placed 'all His affection' in Jesus assures the Christian that God never acts out of compulsion, but out of free benevolence. It is a word of divine love — one that tells us that we are pleasing to God, not by our merits, but through Christ.

sens: The favorable will of someone, their benevolent assent
What one wishes, what pleases their heart
The generous intention one forms for someone
The satisfaction, the pleasure one experiences
G2107.detail:
1. Good pleasure primarily expresses someone's favorable will towards an action or a person. It is not just a decision, but a decision that comes from the heart, accompanied by contentment. In Matthew 11:26, Jesus says: "I praise you because you have chosen this," meaning that the Father decided this with satisfaction.
2. The word then designates what one wishes, what deeply pleases their heart. In Romans 10:1, Paul speaks of the "desire of my heart" for the Israelites to be saved: it is his earnest desire.
3. It can also refer to the generous intention one conceives for someone else. In Ephesians 1:5, we are predestined "according to the good pleasure of His will": God has chosen us in advance with kindness.
4. Finally, good pleasure expresses the delight, the satisfaction one feels. In Luke 2:14, "peace on earth among those with whom He is pleased": these are the men whom God rejoices in.
G2107.origine: The word comes from the Greek εὖ (well) and δοκέω (to believe, to judge, to esteem). It literally means "to judge favorably" or "to be content with." In Hebrew, the word רָצוֹן (ratzôn) that this term often translates evokes also what "pleases," what one "approves." The Greek root suggests a judgment of the heart, not a mere imposed decision.
G2107.emploi: The word εὐδοκία appears 9 times in the provided usages, mostly in the Gospels and Paul's epistles. In Luke (2:14, 10:21), it expresses what pleases the Father and His benevolent will. In Romans 10:1, it is Paul's sincere wish. In Ephesians (1:5, 1:9), it characterizes God's salvific purpose, formulated with love. In Philippians 2:13, it is God's generous will in us. Its meaning always nuances between active will and heart's contentment, never towards a mere cold decision.
G2107.portee: The good pleasure of God is a word of comfort for the Christian: their salvation is not due to chance or a distant calculation, but to the benevolent heart of the Father. Understanding that we are predestined "according to His good pleasure" means that we are loved, chosen with joy. For Paul, expressing his earnest wishes shows that prayer and the desire for good for others reflect this divine benevolence.

sens: Action of doing good to someone, serving them
Advantage, benefit received
Act of kindness, charity towards others
G2108.detail: 1. A benefit is primarily a concrete act through which one helps someone by responding to their need. In Acts 4:9, Peter speaks of the miracle of healing the beggar as a "benefit granted to a sick man": it is a good and useful intervention that alleviates suffering. 2. It is also the advantage or benefit that the helped person receives — the positive result of this act. 3. More broadly, the word designates any manifestation of kindness, this disposition of the heart to do good to others without expecting anything in return. In 1 Timothy 6:2, serving one's Christian masters consists of doing them "good" with dedication, because one loves them.
G2108.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: "eu" (good) and "ergon" (action, work). Literally, it is a "good action." In classical Greek, it designates the generous action of a public benefactor. The family of the word includes "euergetes" (benefactor), one who acts for the good of others. It is a rich word that links action to morality: doing good means acting in a good way.
G2108.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament. In Acts 4:9, in the context of Peter being questioned by the Sanhedrin about the healing of the beggar at the Beautiful Gate, he qualifies a miracle as a benevolent work towards a sick man. In 1 Timothy 6:2, Paul exhorts Christian slaves to serve their believing masters "all the better" by doing good to them with heart. In both cases, the word emphasizes the concrete and positive action, but also the generous intention behind it.
G2108.portee: This word reminds the Christian that doing good is not a distant obligation, but a visible and tangible act that relieves, heals, and builds the community. For the believer, serving others — even one's superiors — becomes a "benefit" when done out of love and dedication. It is an invitation to see in every act of help a manifestation of God's goodness.

sens: To perform generous and benevolent actions towards someone
To exercise a power of healing and liberation
To manifest the powerful action of God in the world
G2109.detail:
1. The word designates the action of doing good, that is, accomplishing acts of generosity and kindness towards others. It is a concrete activity: helping, healing, liberating from misery or illness. In Acts 10:38, Jesus went about "doing good" — He traveled through villages sowing benefit upon benefit.
2. More specifically, to do good encompasses healing and deliverance: Acts 10:38 shows Jesus who "was doing good" by healing "all who were under the power of the devil." Good is not a moral abstraction, but a power that liberates and restores.
3. This doing good is the visible expression of God's power: in Acts 10:38, Peter emphasizes that God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit and power, and it is this anointing that enabled Him to do good. Thus, it is the divine action that passes through Christ and transforms the world.
G2109.origine: The word comes from the Greek word "euergetes" (benefactor), composed of "eu" (good) and "ergon" (work, action). It etymologically designates one who accomplishes a good work. This vocabulary was common in the Greek world to honor those who showed generosity towards cities or peoples. The Bible uses it to qualify the action of Jesus as that of a true benefactor — not in the Greek political sense, but in the spiritual and eternal sense.
G2109.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 10:38. Peter uses it to summarize the public ministry of Jesus: He "went about doing good." This summary is particularly remarkable as it is addressed to the centurion Cornelius and his household, pagans who may not know who Jesus is. Peter chooses this universal word — to do good — to make the nature of Christ's ministry understandable to them: it is a work of visible liberation and healing for all. The context shows that doing good means concretely healing the sick and casting out demons.
G2109.portee: This word invites the believer to see Christ as the true benefactor, the one whose action truly transforms the human condition. In speaking of Jesus who "went about doing good," Peter does not dissolve the message of salvation into a vague morality: he states that authentic good comes through healing, deliverance, and the power of the Spirit. For the Christian, this means that serving God is to do concrete good: to heal, to liberate, to restore, reflecting God's powerful goodness in a world marked by suffering and oppression.

sens: one who does good to someone
a leader or prince who grants benefits to their people
G2110.detail:
1. A benefactor is someone who does good to others, who serves, who gives or bestows benefits. The Greek word primarily evokes a generous and positive action towards a person or group.
2. In political and royal contexts, it is a title of honor given to kings and leaders who show generosity towards their people. Jesus uses this term in Luke 22:25 with a hint of irony: the kings of the nations dominate their subjects but are called 'benefactors', as if their power were an act of kindness — whereas, Jesus says, the opposite should prevail among his disciples.
G2110.origine: The word comes from the Greek root eu (good) and ergon (work, action). Literally, it is one who performs a 'good deed'. The word was widely used in Greco-Roman times to honor generous public figures. It can be found in inscriptions and administrative texts from antiquity to designate patrons and benefactors of cities.
G2110.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 22:25. Jesus uses it during the Last Supper to criticize the governing style of pagan kings. The context shows that this flattering title — 'benefactors' — actually conceals an exercise of power based on domination. Jesus contrasts this with the true service that his disciples should practice.
G2110.portee: This passage invites the disciple to reconsider their relationship to power and authority. The true 'benefactor' is not the one who dominates while seeking honor, but the one who serves and humbles themselves. It is an important lesson on the reversal of values in the Kingdom: Christian greatness is measured by service, not by prestige.

sens: Suitable for use, ready to serve
Capable of fulfilling a function or task
Appropriate for a destiny or purpose
G2111.detail:
1. The word primarily describes something arranged for use: land that receives regular rain produces 'useful' grass for those who cultivate it (Hebrews 6:7). It conveys the idea of something prepared, available, and functional.

2. It also applies to a person capable of fulfilling a function: one who puts their hand to the plow but looks back 'is not fit' for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62). It refers to an aptitude, a suitability for a task or state.

3. Finally, the word expresses the idea of a correspondence between a person or thing and its destination: to be fit for something means to be adapted to it, to be destined for it. The phrase 'fit for' marks this necessary adequacy.
G2111.origine: The word comes from the root 'eu' (good) and 'tithémi' (to place, to set). It literally designates what is 'well placed', that is, suitably arranged, positioned to be useful. The Greek root is related to the verb 'to place': the word retains the idea of preparation, of being put in a state.
G2111.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always to express an aptitude or suitability. In Luke 9:62, Jesus uses it to describe one who is not 'fit' for the kingdom of God — one who looks back after putting their hand to the plow lacks the focus and loyalty required. In Hebrews 6:7, it qualifies the 'useful' grass produced by well-watered land: it is grass that serves its purpose, that benefits the cultivators. In Luke 14:35 (not cited here but in the references), the context is similar. The word always evokes a functional or spiritual adaptation.
G2111.portee: This word reminds the reader that the disciple of Jesus must be entirely 'fit' for the kingdom — fully committed, without looking back, without distraction. There is a requirement for adequacy between who we are and what we are called to. It is an invitation to complete availability.

sens: Without delay, at once, right at that moment
Quickly, without waiting
As soon as, at the moment when (temporal conjunction)
G2112.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the absence of delay: something occurs at that moment, without waiting. When the apostles hear Jesus' call, 'immediately they left their nets and followed him' (Matthew 4:20) — there is no downtime between the call and obedience. Or when a soldier pierces Christ's side, 'immediately there came out blood and water' (John 19:34): it is immediate, without interval.
2. The word can also emphasize the rapid succession of events: one thing follows another without pause. After his resurrection, Jesus vanishes 'immediately' after saying to the disciples 'Peace be with you' (John 13:32), marking the fluid sequence of events.
3. In narrative contexts, immediately functions as a temporal marker that connects two actions: 'Early in the morning, the chief priests held a council' (Mark 15:1) — it is at dawn that what follows begins.
G2112.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective euthy (εὐθύς), which means 'straight, direct'. The adverb immediately inherits this idea of directness: an action that goes straight to its goal, without detour or delay. It is an image of rectitude applied to time. The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) sometimes renders the Hebrew pita'om (פִּתְאוֹם), which means 'suddenly, all at once' (Job 5:3). This Greek root εὐθ- is found in the name Eutychos and in other words expressing straightness or directness.
G2112.emploi: The word appears 92 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in the four Gospels (very frequent in Mark and Luke) and in Acts. It generally serves to mark rapid transitions in the narrative: disciples who leave everything to follow Jesus (Matthew 4:20, Mark 1:18), instant healings (Matthew 8:3, Luke 5:13), sudden events (a possessed person convulsed, Mark 1:26). In John, it appears less frequently but carries particular weight (resurrection, John 5:9; Jesus recognized by Peter, John 13:30). The word also sometimes translates 'as' in the temporal sense ('as soon as morning'), broadening its scope to the notion of the moment when something begins.
G2112.portee: This word reminds us that faith and obedience in the Bible do not linger: the apostles who respond to Jesus' call 'immediately' leave everything to follow him (Matthew 4:20). Healings occur without delay when Jesus acts, demonstrating his power and immediate presence. For the Christian reader, immediately is an invitation to see how the Gospel operates in history without delay: God speaks and things happen.

sens: Sail in a straight line from one port to another without detour
Travel by sea taking the most direct route
G2113.detail:
1. This verb literally describes the journey of a ship that follows a direct route between two ports. In Acts 16:11, Paul and his companions "sail directly to Samothrace" from Troas: they do not stop along the way, they go straight to the goal. It is a technical term from maritime vocabulary that emphasizes the simplicity and efficiency of the journey.
2. Figuratively, the expression evokes any direct advance toward a goal, without unnecessary detours. In Acts 21:1, after parting from the elders of Ephesus, Paul "goes directly to Cos": the word reveals the intention to continue his journey without interruption, as if guided by a clear purpose.
G2113.origine: The word combines two Greek roots: "eu" (well, straight) and "dromos" (course, path). It thus refers to a "straight" route or course. This term belongs to the language of Greek sailors, who used this expression to describe non-stop navigations. The same prefix "eu" (good, straight) appears in many biblical words: "gospel" (good message), "eucharist" (thanksgiving). The central idea is always one of straightness or correct direction.
G2113.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in the book of Acts, in chapters 16 and 21. Both occurrences recount maritime journeys of the Apostle Paul in the eastern Mediterranean: first to Samothrace (16:11), then to Cos (21:1). In both cases, the word emphasizes that Paul and his team do not linger but go straight to their destination, in accordance with the divine plan of their mission. The term is specifically maritime and is never used figuratively in the preserved biblical texts.
G2113.portee: This word shows how Paul conducted his missionary journeys with determination and clarity of purpose. The Christian reader can see a lesson here: the life of faith, like navigation, benefits from having a clear and direct direction, without straying onto detours. It is an invitation to faithfulness and constancy in the service of God.

sens: Have a light and serene heart, without fear or anxiety
Be filled with confidence and assurance in the face of a trial
Exhort someone to regain their serenity and calm
G2114.detail:
1. The word first evokes the state of a person who has a light heart, who breathes serenity — it is an inner disposition of peace and confidence. In Acts 27:25, Paul says to the frightened sailors: "take heart," inviting each one to this tranquility of mind in the face of the impending shipwreck.
2. This serenity arises from a deep trust, even in the storm: Paul addresses terrified men and calls them to be "of good cheer" because he firmly believes in God's promise (Acts 27:22).
3. The word can also refer to the invitation, the exhortation addressed to someone to reassure them: it is a call to leave fear and enter into trust, as seen in James who encourages the joyful to sing (James 5:13).
G2114.origine: The word comes from two roots: εὖ (well, good) and θυμός (the heart, the soul, the seat of emotions). Its primary image is that of a soul or heart in good condition, serene and confident. It is a classical Greek word, used by tragedians to express serenity in the face of trials.
G2114.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, all in contexts of trial or joy. In Acts 27, Paul uses it twice to reassure the crew of a ship in a storm, basing this confidence on the certainty of God's protection. In James 5:13, it marks the attitude of one who lives in joy and gives thanks. In all cases, the word denotes a state of the soul that can be maintained or restored, particularly important when going through anxiety or celebrating the good.
G2114.portee: This word invites the Christian to an inner disposition of trust and calm, even in the face of life's storms. It is not naivety, but it rests on the certainty of God's protection and faithfulness, as Paul shows to the sailors. It is also expressed in the joy of one who gives thanks — it is a distinctive mark of one who lives their faith with assurance.

sens: state of one who has a light spirit, free from fear
calm confidence in the face of a difficult situation
disposition to encourage others
G2115.detail:
1. The word first paints an inner state: one who has a light spirit, without anxiety or deep trouble. It is a kind of natural serenity, as if one sees life from the bright side. In Acts 27:36, after the storm at sea, the sailors "take courage": they regain that lightness of heart that fear had dissipated.
2. But this courage is not naive insouciance: it is a calm confidence, capable of standing firm in adversity. In Acts 24:10, Paul presents himself before the governor with this "confidence" — he does not tremble, he looks the judge in the face because he has an inner assurance, even though his case is dangerous.
3. The word also evokes the ability to maintain or inspire this state in oneself and in others: a spirit that refuses despair and communicates its serenity.
G2115.origine: The word comes from eu- (well) and thumos (the heart, the soul, the inner disposition). This compound was already found in ancient Greek poets (Homer, Aeschylus) to designate a man of good character or good morals. It is a learned and literary word, which expresses not a violent feeling, but a stable and deep quality of the soul.
G2115.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke (Acts). In both cases, it refers to courage or confidence in the face of danger or uncertainty. In Acts 27:36, Paul has just reassured the passengers of a ship about to sink: at these words, the men regain courage and eat — it is the return to normalcy of one who is no longer afraid. In Acts 24:10, it is Paul himself who faces the tribunal with this calm confidence. The word thus depicts less an emotion than an inner virtue: the stability of one who does not let themselves be downcast.
G2115.portee: This word speaks to the inner peace that the Christian can find in Christ, even in the face of the worst trials. Paul did not choose to go through a storm or to stand trial, but instead of succumbing to panic, he maintains a peaceful spirit — it is the image of a faith that holds firm. For us, it reminds us that true courage is not the absence of fear, but the ability to remain clear-headed and confident when everything collapses.

sens: To orient something in a direction, to guide its course
To make straight, to level a path or road
To command, to control the movement of something
G2116.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to orient, to guide: it is to direct something towards a destination. James 3:4 illustrates this well: a small rudder "directs" a large ship at the will of the pilot, that is, according to his desire — the rudder commands the trajectory of the entire ship.

2. In a more concrete sense, the word means to make straight, to level. This is the role of the rudder which "straightens" the ship towards its course. John 1:23 uses this word in the sense of preparing and leveling a path: "Make straight the way of the Lord" — the image evokes the Exodus, when preparing the passage of a king by making the road smooth and passable.

3. The two meanings converge: to direct is also to rectify, to set straight towards the goal. The rudder directs the ship by straightening it towards its course; the message of the Forerunner levels the path by preparing hearts to receive the Lord.
G2116.origine: The word comes from the adjective εὐθύς ("straight," "direct"), whose root evokes what is aligned and without deviation. The Latin translation is "dirigere" (to direct). In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates Hebrew words like נָטָה (to incline, to direct) and יָשַׁר (to make straight, to set in order). The word always carries the idea of rectitude and orientation towards a goal.
G2116.emploi: The verb εὐθύνω appears twice in the New Testament. In James 3:4, it describes how a small rudder directs a large ship — it is an image of domination and control, the small commanding the large. In John 1:23, it appears in the Forerunner's quotation (Isaiah 40:3): "Make straight the way of the Lord" — here, to direct and to level converge to denote spiritual preparation, the setting in order of hearts. In both uses, the word evokes an action that rectifies, that sets in a straight line towards a goal.
G2116.portee: This verb reminds Christians that only God truly masters our direction. Just as the small rudder directs the large ship, a small reaction of the heart can straighten our entire path. John 1:23 also shows that preparing to receive Jesus first involves leveling internal obstacles, rectifying our intentions and dispositions.

sens: That does not deviate, that goes straight ahead (of a path, of a road)
That is rectified, straightened (of a curved or uneven surface)
That is sincere, loyal, without deviation (of the heart, of the will)
Immediately, without delay (adverbial use: straightway)
G2117.detail:
1. The primary meaning is geometric: a line or path that does not zigzag, that goes straight ahead. It is distinguished from winding paths. When John the Baptist cries in the wilderness: "Prepare the way of the Lord, make His paths straight" (Matthew 3:3), the word "straight" refers to a straight path, without unnecessary curves.

2. By extension, the word also describes what is straightened or leveled: a mountain or hill that disappears, a bumpy road that becomes smooth. In Luke 3:5, what was "crooked will be made straight" — the image is that of a way being corrected, made passable.

3. In a moral and spiritual sense, "straight" qualifies a sincere heart, an unfeigned intention. When Peter says to Simon the magician: "Your heart is not right before God" (Acts 8:21), he asserts that Simon lacks sincerity, moral uprightness. It is the opposite of a twisted or deceptive attitude.

4. As an adverb, the word means "immediately," "straightaway" — an action that follows without delay. Although this adverbial use is attested in Greek ("straightway"), it does not appear in the provided Segond uses for this specific word.
G2117.origine: The Greek word εὐθύς (euthus) comes from an Indo-European root expressing straightness, the absence of curve. In Hebrew, it often translates יָשַׁר (yashar), which means "to be straight" or "to be just." The starting image is physical and geometric — a line without deviation — before extending to the moral domain: what does not deviate from the rules, what is loyal and true. The same family of words in Greek produces compounds and derivatives related to straightness, rectification.
G2117.emploi: The word appears mainly in three contexts. First, in linking Isaiah to the synoptics (Matthew, Mark, Luke), it designates the paths that must be leveled before the coming of the Lord — here, a figurative language to describe the preparation of the heart. Next, in Acts 8:21, it qualifies the heart of Simon the magician as lacking moral uprightness before God — a call to spiritual sincerity. In Acts 9:11, "the straight street" is the name of a street in Damascus, perhaps named for its straight layout. Finally, in Acts 13:10 and 2 Peter 2:15, the word describes straight or twisted paths or ways of living in a moral sense.
G2117.portee: This word reminds believers that preparation to meet the Lord is not primarily a matter of geography, but of the sincerity of the heart. A "straight" heart before God is a heart without duplicity, without ulterior motives. The contrast between straight paths and crooked paths invites us to examine our intentions: do we live in simplicity and loyalty towards God, or do we hide behind detours and lies? It is an invitation to spiritual transparency.

sens: The character of one who is straight, just, and honest
Moral uprightness and integrity
Justice rendered with impartiality and respect for the law
G2118.detail:
1. Equity denotes the moral uprightness and integrity of one who acts without deviation, without malice. It is to be straight, in both a literal and figurative sense. In Hebrews 1:8, the scepter of Christ is a "scepter of equity," an image of a king who governs with justice and uprightness, without favoritism and without corruption.

2. It is also justice rendered with impartiality: the character of one who judges without leaning to one side or the other, who is not corrupted. Equity stands in opposition to perversity, malice, and the twisting of justice.

3. In royal or divine context, equity becomes the fundamental attribute of legitimate power: a king or a God who governs in equity is worthy of trust and respect.
G2118.origine: The Greek word comes from the root "euthus" which means "straight," "correct," "without deviation." This image of straightness is first physical (a straight line) and then moral (a straight conduct). In Hebrew, the parallel biblical word is "yoscher" or its derivatives, which also evoke the idea of rectitude and straightness. The word family includes other Greek terms related to straightness and honesty.
G2118.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 1:8, in a quotation from Psalm 45 applied to Christ. The context is that of a divine declaration from the Father to the Son: the throne of Christ is eternal, and His scepter is a scepter of equity. This uniqueness underscores the theological importance of the passage: equity is presented as the essence of Christ's divine reign, which establishes the absolute legitimacy of His authority. The word is rare in biblical Greek, but heavy with meaning when it appears.
G2118.portee: For Christians, this equity of Christ is a foundation of trust: it assures that He who reigns over the Church and the universe judges and governs without injustice, without favoritism, with absolute rectitude. This invites inner peace in the face of His sovereignty and the aspiration to imitate this uprightness in our relationships with others.

sens: To have leisure, availability to do something
To have the opportunity, favorable possibility to do something
To spend one's free time on an activity
G2119.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the fact of having free time, being able to rest or relax. In Mark 6:31, Jesus invites his disciples to find time to eat and rest, as they did not even have time to do so — they were too busy with the crowds.
2. It also means to have the opportunity or possibility to do something. In 1 Corinthians 16:12, Paul explains that Apollos did not have the opportunity to come now — he would need to wait for a more favorable moment.
3. The word can finally describe the act of dedicating one's free time to a particular activity. In Acts 17:21, the Athenians spent all their time discussing the news — it was their usual leisure, their constant concern.
G2119.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek expression meaning "to have free time" or "to have ease." The root ἐύ (eu) means "well" and καιρός (kairos) means "opportune moment, occasion." It is a classical word, used by ancient Greek historians like Polybius. It expresses the idea of having the chance and freedom to do something at the right time.
G2119.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament. In Mark 6:31, it describes the disciples' lack of free time, being too busy. In 1 Corinthians 16:12, Paul uses it to indicate that a person currently does not have the possibility or does not wish to seize the opportunity. In Acts 17:21, it designates the time the Athenians spent listening to and commenting on the news — a habit, a mental leisure. The word balances between two meanings: having available time and having a favorable opportunity to act.
G2119.portee: This word reminds us that time is a precious, often limited resource. For the Christian, it raises the question of how we use our moments of leisure and freedom: what do we dedicate our availability to? It also invites us to recognize that some opportunities come from God — it is not always our will, but also providence that determines the right moment to act.

sens: A propitious moment, well-suited for what one wants to do
An opportune time when circumstances allow for action
An opening, a chance to succeed in what one has prepared
G2120.detail:
1. The word first designates a moment that perfectly suits an action — an instant when everything aligns for one to do what one wishes. Judas was looking for a "favorable opportunity" to betray Jesus (Matthew 26:16, Luke 22:6): he was waiting for the right moment when the crowd would not be present and the act would be possible.
2. It is also the time chosen by the one who acts, the opening they are watching for. The favorable opportunity is therefore less a chance than a window of time where obstacles are removed and where action becomes feasible.
G2120.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek "eukairos" (composed of "eu," well, and "kairos," moment, occasion). It literally expresses "a well-chosen moment." This Greek root "kairos" is at the heart of the biblical notion of time: not a measured time that passes ("chronos"), but a moment filled with meaning, a season given by God. The favorable opportunity is a kairos — a decisive instant.
G2120.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew and Luke, and in the same context: Judas's betrayal. In Matthew 26:16 and Luke 22:6, after agreeing to betray Jesus, Judas "was looking for a favorable opportunity." This is not an impulsive act: he waits for the strategically optimal moment when the sleepy disciples cannot intervene and the crowd will not see him. The expression emphasizes the calculated preparation of the betrayal.
G2120.portee: This word reminds us that timing matters in our decisions and actions. Judas was waiting for the favorable opportunity to betray: the Bible thus shows how sin is patiently prepared, watching for the weak moment. For the Christian, it is an invitation to remain vigilant and not to create space for evil — but also to recognize that only God masters true time and even turns our weaknesses to His purpose.

sens: That arrives at the right moment, timely
That suits the present situation
That is favorable, propitious
G2121.detail:
1. An opportune moment is one that comes just when it is needed, like a door that opens exactly when one needs it. In Mark 6:21, an "opportune day" arrives for Herod at the time of his birthday feast: it is the chosen moment, favorable for a request or decision.
2. The word designates what is appropriate, suitable for the given moment. An opportune help is one that arrives when it is truly needed, at the critical moment. In Hebrews 4:16, one can find mercy and grace "to be helped in our needs": God's help is opportune, it comes at the moment we need it most.
3. Underlying these two meanings, opportune evokes the idea of what is favorable, without obstacles. It is the moment when circumstances play in our favor.
G2121.origine: The Greek word comes from "eu" (well) and "kairos" (the moment, the opportune time, the critical time). It describes what is well-timed, what coincides with the kairos. The Greek notion of kairos is that of the moment filled with meaning, opposed to chronos, the time that flows mechanically. Opportune thus captures what harmonizes with this decisive moment.
G2121.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament translated by the Segond. In Mark 6:21, it qualifies the moment of Herod's feast as propitious for an important request. In Hebrews 4:16, it characterizes divine help as intervening at the moment of our needs. The context is always that of a happy convergence between the moment and the circumstance.
G2121.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that God arranges times and seasons according to His wisdom. It reminds us that God's help, grace, and mercy are never late: they always arrive at the opportune moment, when we need them most. It is a word of trust in divine providence.

sens: At the right moment, when circumstances are favorable
At a propitious and well-chosen moment
In contrast: without waiting for the ideal moment
G2122.detail:
1. The word describes an action that occurs at the precise moment when it can succeed or produce its effect. Judas seeks a favorable opportunity to betray Jesus discreetly, without attracting the crowd (Mark 14:11) — he waits for the right moment.
2. It is the idea of acting when the opportunity presents itself, when the conditions are met. To insist "at all times, favorable or not" (2 Timothy 4:2) means: even when it is not the ideal moment, one must proclaim the Gospel — which emphasizes that "favorable" means "when it is propitious."
3. The word opposes the idea of acting at the wrong moment, hastily or without discernment. This is why Paul insists to Timothy: one must preach both in opportune times and in difficult times.
G2122.origine: The Greek word εὐκαίρως (eukairōs) comes from εὖ ("well") + καιρός ("moment, opportune time"). Καιρός designates not the time that passes (chronos), but the particular instant, the occasion, the decisive moment. Εὐκαίρως literally means "well-timed, appropriately." It is an adverb formed from the adjective εὔκαιρος which also appears in the Bible.
G2122.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament. In Mark 14:11, it characterizes the moment Judas is waiting for to accomplish his betrayal: an opportunity that circumstances offer him. In 2 Timothy 4:2, Paul uses the phrase "at all times, favorable or not" to show that the servant of God should not only wait for ideal moments: he must preach constantly, whether it is easy or difficult. The adverb thus emphasizes the importance of timing, the discernment of the right moment.
G2122.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that discerning the opportune moment is important: acting out of time can fail or cause harm. But it also invites us not to be enslaved by the perfection of circumstances — Timothy's example shows that one must witness even when it is not easy. It is a balance between wisdom and urgency.

sens: That does not require effort, that is accomplished without difficulty
That is easier to achieve than another thing
That is self-evident, that imposes itself naturally
G2123.detail:
1. The word describes an action that is done without effort, without difficulty. It is what costs little to do. When the disciples ask Jesus what is easier — to say to a paralytic, 'Your sins are forgiven' or 'Get up and walk' — they suspect that it is easy to pronounce words, while giving an order that is realized is more difficult (Mark 2:9).
2. The word is often in the comparative form: 'easier'. Jesus uses it to show that a certain reality is more accessible than another. It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God: this shocking comparison reveals that the impossible for the rich is more possible than the impossible for the camel (Matthew 19:24).
3. The word can also indicate what imposes itself as a natural consequence. It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of a letter of the law to fall: in other words, the destruction of the universe is more probable than the slightest invalidation of God's Law (Luke 16:17).
G2123.origine: The word comes from the Greek εὖ ('well') and κόπος ('work, effort'). The starting image is that of work done well, without pain. The adjective literally means 'that has good work' or 'that does not cost effort'. It is a classical Greek term to describe what is easy or convenient. The root κόπος also appears in French words like 'copie' (copy work) and conveys the idea of a task that is accomplished more or less easily.
G2123.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, especially in the first three Gospels. Jesus uses it in the comparative form in questions and statements to unsettle those who listen to him. In Matthew 9:5 and Mark 2:9, he challenges the scribes by asking what is easier to say: to forgive sins or to heal — the question reveals that easy words often hide a powerlessness of the soul. In Matthew 19:24, Mark 10:25, and Luke 18:25, Jesus repeats that the entry of the rich into the kingdom is more difficult than the impossible of the camel and the needle. In Luke 16:17, he asserts that the stability of divine Law is more certain than the end of the world. Everywhere, the word serves not to comfort, but to strike the mind: what seems easy may be superficial, and what appears impossible may reveal the power of God.
G2123.portee: This word invites us not to confuse the ease of words with the reality of transformed hearts. For a believer, it reminds us that true conversion requires more than verbal assent. It also teaches us to recognize the absolute stability of God's Word, more enduring than the world itself: what is difficult for the rich man — entering the kingdom — reveals not a weakness of God, but a heart requirement that no one can bypass.

sens: Respectful fear of God
Religious reverence
Circumspect prudence in relation to God
The attitude of one who fears God and acts seriously
G2124.detail: 1. Piety primarily means a respectful fear — not the fear of punishment, but the respect mixed with wonder before the greatness and authority of God. It is the inner state of one who knows they stand before the Lord (Hebrews 12:28: 'let us receive the unshakable kingdom, and show gratitude by offering to God an acceptable worship, with reverence'). 2. This piety also implies a certain restraint, a prudence: one who possesses it pays attention not to offend God, acting with discretion and seriousness in sacred matters. 3. It can take the form of sincere devotion, as when Jesus prays with tears and cries (Hebrews 5:7): piety expresses it in a sincere and respectful abandonment. 4. It is a global attitude of the heart and life, the opposite of indifference or levity towards divine realities.
G2124.origine: The word comes from the Greek 'eu' (well) and 'labein' (to seize, to fear), literally 'well-placed fear'. It thus denotes a wise and justified fear. In ancient Greek, it initially meant prudence or discretion; the New Testament has used it in the more religious sense of reverential fear of God. In the Greek Old Testament, it sometimes translates Hebrew words evoking fear or concern.
G2124.emploi: The word 'piety' appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Hebrews. In Hebrews 5:7, Paul describes how Jesus, 'in the days of his flesh', prayed 'with piety' — showing that even the Son of God manifested this respectful fear towards his Father. In Hebrews 12:28, the apostle exhorts believers to 'serve God with piety', by offering a worship that is pleasing to him. In these two contexts, piety qualifies the authentic attitude of the believer towards the living and holy God.
G2124.portee: Piety reminds us that our relationship with God is not a matter of levity or indifference. It is an attitude of respectful love, where the fear of the Lord and reverence go hand in hand. Even Christ prayed with this piety towards his Father: it is therefore a model for us. It invites us to seek to please God in everyday life, with seriousness and sincerity.

sens: To have a fear mixed with respect and reverence towards someone or something
To take care, to be cautious, to be on guard
To honor by submitting with fear
G2125.detail: 1. To fear with respect means to experience a fear that is not servile or panicked, but mixed with veneration and obedience. It is the reaction of someone who recognizes the authority, holiness, or power of a superior person or reality. Noah, 'moved by respectful fear', in Hebrews 11:7, illustrates this attitude: he does not tremble in terror, but with a pious fear that drives him to obey divine warnings and build the ark. 2. To take care or be cautious means to be alert, to pay attention to danger or what may happen, and to act with circumspection. This meaning aligns with the first when prudence arises from reverence. 3. To honor by submitting with fear means to recognize the excellence or holiness of another through an attitude of fearful deference, not by calculation or servile fear, but through sincere love and respect.
G2125.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and expresses the idea of 'keeping away' or 'taking care' (from εὖ, well, and λαβεῖν, to take). It describes an attitude of fearful attention. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this word translates several Hebrew words related to the pious fear of God and prudence. The central notion is that of a fear mixed with respect, quite different from mere terror.
G2125.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Hebrews 11:7, where it qualifies Noah's respectful fear in the face of divine words. This context shows us that the word denotes a pious fear, an active reverence that drives the one who feels it to obey faithfully. Classical Greek and ancient translations (Old Testament in Greek) use this verb to describe reverent fear towards God and caution in the face of dangers. It is a characteristic attitude of authentic faith: not a fear that paralyzes, but a reverence that mobilizes obedience.
G2125.portee: This word reminds the believer that true faith is accompanied by a respectful fear of God. It is not a servile fear that crushes, but a living reverence that inspires obedience and action. Noah's example teaches that this fear, far from paralyzing, liberates and enables one to accomplish great things for God. For the Christian, it invites us to honor God with a heart filled with both respect and trust.

sens: One who fears God and scrupulously observes His law
One who acts with reverence and respect towards sacred things
One who is prudent and cautious in their decisions
G2126.detail: 1. A pious man is someone who sincerely fears God and takes great care to respect His law. Simeon in Luke 2:25 is a model of this: he is described as "righteous and pious," who patiently awaited the Messiah, showing that being pious means living in deep accordance with God's promises and requirements. 2. The word also evokes an attitude of reverence and respect towards God and His worship. The pious men of Acts 2:5 came from all nations to Jerusalem, likely for religious festivals; their piety draws them towards God. Similarly, those who buried Stephen (Acts 8:2) acted with respect towards sacred customs, even regarding a man they did not understand. 3. Piety also includes a dimension of prudence and caution: one who fears God is careful not to offend Him, reflecting before acting. Ananias (Acts 22:12) is described as pious "according to the law," which shows that he walks attentively on the path that God has laid out.
G2126.origine: The Greek word comes from "eu" (well) and "labein" (to seize, to take), the original image being that of "seizing well," meaning to have a good grasp on things, to be stable and prudent. In ancient Greek, it initially meant "prudent" or "cautious." In the Greek Bible, it gained a strong religious dimension: to be pious is to grasp well, to understand well, and to observe what God requires. It often translates the Hebrew "hasid" (חָסִיד) in the Greek Old Testament, which designates a friend of God, one who is faithful to Him with love and devotion.
G2126.emploi: The word "pious" appears 4 times in the New Testament, always with a positive connotation and often to qualify faithful Jews. In Luke 2:25, Simeon is the archetype of the pious: righteous towards men, pious towards God, he lives in expectation of the Messiah. In Acts 2:5, the pious Jews are those who left their homeland to come to Jerusalem to celebrate; they form the core of those who will listen to Peter at Pentecost. In Acts 8:2, piety is expressed in the act of mourning and burying with dignity, respecting customs even in the face of the disruption that Stephen caused. Finally, Ananias (Acts 22:12) combines his piety with a good testimony among all, showing that authentic piety is evident in life.
G2126.portee: Piety is not a vague religious sentimentality, but a fear of God that produces obedience, reverence, and moral prudence. It draws one towards God and His worship. For today's Christian, this word invites the cultivation of a serious relationship with God, based on respect for His word and attention to His commandments, rather than settling for an outward appearance of religion.

sens: To praise someone, to speak well of them before God
To invoke God's favor upon someone, to wish them well
To grant goods, prosperity (when God is the subject)
To give thanks, to express gratitude before eating
To render a favorable judgment on someone or something
G2127.detail:
1. To praise someone is to speak well of them, to acknowledge their excellence before God and others. This is how the disciples praise Jesus (Luke 24:53: "they were continually in the temple, praising God"), or how James reproaches those who bless and curse with the same mouth (James 3:9).
2. To invoke divine favor upon someone is to wish them well and ask God to fill them with His gifts. Jesus teaches to bless those who curse us (Matthew 5:44), and the patriarchs blessed their sons to ensure their prosperity (Hebrews 11:20-21).
3. When God is the one who blesses, He dispenses His favors: He blesses believers in Christ by granting them spiritual blessings and goods (Ephesians 1:3: "God has blessed us with every spiritual blessing").
4. To give thanks before eating is to thank God for the food before sharing it (Mark 6:41: "He gave thanks" before breaking the loaves; Luke 9:16: the same gesture at the meal).
5. To render a favorable judgment is to declare someone or something happy, worthy of praise: "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!" (Luke 13:35; John 12:13).
G2127.origine: The word comes from the Greek eulogos (well-spoken, praiseworthy). The prefix eu- means "well," and logos means "word": it is to speak well of someone. The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses this verb to translate the Hebrew barak, which originally evokes the idea of kneeling in reverence and homage. This Hebrew root is found in the family of the word "blessing" in French.
G2127.emploi: The verb appears about forty times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke and in the epistles. It is used in three main ways: (1) men praise God or bless the name of the Lord (Luke 1:64; Luke 24:53; James 3:9); (2) men bless other men by wishing them well (Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:28; Romans 12:14), particularly the patriarchs bless their sons (Hebrews 7:1; Hebrews 11:20-21); (3) God blesses men by granting them His favors and protection (Acts 3:26; Galatians 3:9; Ephesians 1:3). The verb also designates the act of giving thanks before meals (Mark 6:41; Luke 9:16; 1 Corinthians 10:16). The adjective "blessed" (eulogetos) describes one upon whom the blessing rests.
G2127.portee: This verb opens to the Christian the posture of praise, thanksgiving, and intercession. To bless God is to acknowledge His goodness and greatness; to bless others is to follow Jesus' example by wishing well even to those who do us harm (Matthew 5:44). It is also to receive with gratitude the gifts of God, who blesses us in Christ with all kinds of blessings.

sens: One who has received a blessing, who is favored by God
One who deserves praise and adoration for His greatness and goodness
Worthy of blessings, an object of divine favor
G2128.detail:
1. A person or a people can be blessed by God, meaning graced with His favors and blessings (Mark 14:61: the blessed God, the one who fills with grace). It is the state of one whom God has chosen to fill with His gifts.
2. God Himself is said to be blessed—not because He receives a blessing from another, but because He is worthy of praise, glorification, and adoration par excellence. He is proclaimed blessed to celebrate His majesty and goodness (Luke 1:68: "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel"). It is a way of praising who He is.
3. The word also expresses that someone or something is favored, deemed worthy of blessing—this is the quality of one who receives or deserves divine blessings.
G2128.origine: The word comes from the verb "to bless" (εὐλογέω) and literally means "one who has been blessed" or "one who deserves blessing." It is formed from the root "eu" (well) and "logos" (word), evoking the word that does good. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it corresponds mainly to the word "barukh" (בָּרוּךְ), which designates one whom God has filled with His favors or one who is worthy of praise.
G2128.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles of Paul and in the Gospels. It is used in two main ways. First, to describe men or a people blessed by God (Mark 14:61, with the absolute "the blessed God"). Secondly, and more often, to proclaim that God is blessed—this is a doxology, an acclamation of praise towards God for His greatness, mercy, and gifts (Luke 1:68, Romans 1:25, Romans 9:5, 2 Corinthians 1:3, 2 Corinthians 11:31, Ephesians 1:3, 1 Peter 1:3). The context is always one of recognition and thanksgiving.
G2128.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that God is the source of all blessing and that He deserves our praise and adoration. When we proclaim God blessed, we confess His goodness, faithfulness, and power to save and fill us with grace. It is an act of faith that unites us with all those in the Bible who have recognized God's majesty and generosity.

sens: Flattering speech or pleasant word
Praise addressed to God or Christ
Action of blessing someone
Favor, good, or gift received from God
Abundance, fertility granted by God
G2129.detail:
1. Flattering speech or pleasant word: it is a sweet word that pleases the one who hears it, often to seduce them. In Romans 16:18, Paul speaks of those who use "flattering blessings" to deceive the naive — they speak well, but their words hide a bad intention.

2. Praise addressed to God or Christ: it is the act of celebrating God, recognizing His glory and power. In Revelation, the heavenly creatures cry out "blessings," that is, praises (Revelation 5:12-13, 7:12) — they exalt the Lord.

3. Action of blessing someone: it is the gesture or word by which one calls good upon someone. The cup of "blessing" in 1 Corinthians 10:16 is the cup over which a prayer of blessing has been said before sharing it.

4. Favor, good, or gift received from God: it is everything that God gives us, all that comes from His grace. Paul says in Romans 15:29 that he will come to the Romans "with a full blessing of Christ" — that is, rich in all the gifts that Christ brings. Ephesians 1:3 lists the "spiritual blessings" that God grants us in Christ.

5. Abundance, fertility granted by God: when one sows "abundantly," one reaps "abundantly" (2 Corinthians 9:6) — the blessing here is the generous harvest, the multiplied fruit that God provides.
G2129.origine: The word comes from the Greek "eu" (good) and "logia" (word): literally "good word." It translates the Hebrew "beraka" (בְּרָכָה), which primarily means "knee" — the image is one of kneeling before someone to wish them well. In Hebrew, to bless is first to bend the knee before God or a king to ask for grace. The word has enriched itself: it designates the action of blessing, then the grace itself.
G2129.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in Hebrews and Revelation. It retains three main uses: (1) blessing as flattering speech (Romans 16:18), (2) blessing as praise to God (Revelation 5:12, 5:13, 7:12), and especially (3) blessing as a gift or grace from God. It is this last sense that predominates: spiritual blessings in Christ (Ephesians 1:3), the blessing of the Gospel (Romans 15:29), the inheritance of the promises (Galatians 3:14), the blessing given instead of the curse (1 Peter 3:9). The word can also designate the concrete fruit, the generous harvest that rain brings (Hebrews 6:7).
G2129.portee: Understanding "blessing" invites the believer to see that God does not cease to act in their favor: it is not a simple pious formula, but the real intervention of God that makes one prosper, forgives, and enriches the soul. It also calls for vigilance: to discern the true word that comes from God from the false flattering word that seduces.

sens: Disposition to generously share what one possesses
Quality of one who gives willingly without self-interested calculation
G2130.detail:
1. It is the disposition of the heart to generously share one's goods with others, without jealously keeping what one has. The word evokes one who has an open heart for giving and who gives willingly. In 1 Timothy 6:18, Paul encourages the rich to cultivate this liberality by giving of their goods to others without counting.
2. It is also the moral quality of one who does not selfishly withhold what they possess, but shares it. This virtue opposes greed and selfish accumulation. Paul speaks here of an active and practical generosity, not just a feeling.
G2130.origine: The Greek word is composed of two parts: "eu" (good) and a root meaning "to share, to give." This composition literally expresses the idea of "giving well" or "giving willingly." It is a rare word in the Greek Bible, used to describe a quality praised among the people of God: that of generously sharing their resources.
G2130.emploi: Paul uses this word only once in the Church, in 1 Timothy 6:18. He uses it to urge wealthy believers to cultivate liberality as one of the distinctive marks of their lives. Paul associates this virtue with other qualities: doing good, being rich in good works, and being generous. It is a practical virtue that is realized through the effective sharing of goods with the poor.
G2130.portee: Liberality calls the believer to a change of heart regarding their possessions. It reminds us that receiving from God means being called to give generously. This virtue breaks natural selfishness and unites us with others. It reflects the love of Christ who emptied Himself for our salvation.

sens: Mother of Timothy
G2131.detail: Eunice is the mother of Timothy, the young collaborator of the apostle Paul. She is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Timothy 1:5, where Paul reminds Timothy that sincere faith first dwelled in his grandmother Lois, then in his mother Eunice, before residing in Timothy himself.
G2131.origine: The Greek name Eunikē literally means "good victory" (eu-: good, and nikē: victory). It is a common name in the Greco-Roman world, borne by several ancient women. Here, this name designates the mother of Timothy, a woman of faith who transmitted her trust in God to her son.
G2131.emploi: Eunice appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 1:5. Paul writes to Timothy to encourage him to rekindle the gift of God received in him, and he emphasizes that sincere faith was first transmitted by his grandmother Lois, then by his mother Eunice, before coming to Timothy. This passage shows that Eunice was a faithful believer who played an essential role in the spiritual upbringing of her son, future pastor and worker of Christ.
G2131.portee: Eunice illustrates the crucial role that believing mothers play in passing on faith to their children. Her example reminds Christian parents that their own life of faith is the best inheritance they can leave to their descendants. It also shows how faith can be perpetuated from generation to generation within a family.

sens: To be favorably disposed towards someone
To seek to reconcile with someone
G2132.detail:
1. To be favorably disposed towards someone: it is to have a benevolent, friendly attitude. The word suggests an inclination of the heart and mind towards someone else. In Matthew 5:25, Jesus urges to agree with one's adversary while on the way to the judge, which means adopting a favorable disposition before the conflict escalates.
2. To seek to reconcile with someone: it is to implement this benevolence to restore a broken or tense relationship. It is to act in the direction of peace and rapprochement, rather than allowing hostility to grow.
G2132.origine: The word comes from two Greek elements: "eu" (good) and "nous" (mind, thought). Literally, it means "to have good in mind" or "to be favorably disposed in spirit." This composition reveals the original image: it is an inner state of benevolence and favor towards others. The word occurs only once in the New Testament.
G2132.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew 5:25. Jesus uses it in the context of the Sermon on the Mount, teaching His disciples to resolve conflicts quickly. He says: "Agree with your adversary while you are on the way with him" — that is, be benevolent, seek peace before the conflict becomes irreparable. The context shows that this benevolence is not passive, but active: it consists of taking the initiative for reconciliation.
G2132.portee: Jesus teaches that benevolence and reconciliation should be our priorities in relational conflicts. The believer is called to cultivate a heart disposition favorable towards those with whom they disagree, rather than allowing resentment to settle. It is a call to proactivity in peace: not waiting for the other to take the first step, but seeking to reconcile oneself. This attitude reflects the heart of God, who in Christ took the initiative to reconcile us to Himself.

sens: a favorable and eager disposition to do something
service rendered with enthusiasm and sincerity
cordial devotion towards someone
G2133.detail: 1. Goodwill is this disposition of the heart to do something not out of obligation or constraint, but from a sincere impulse. In 1 Corinthians 7:3, Paul urges husbands and wives to render to each other what they owe "with goodwill": not begrudgingly, but willingly. 2. It is service performed with enthusiasm and eagerness, without grumbling. In Ephesians 6:7, slaves are to serve their masters "with eagerness," as if they were serving the Lord Himself: the heart is in it, it is a living and joyful service. 3. It also expresses cordial devotion, this sincere kindness one has towards someone — acting for their real good, not out of mere mechanical duty.
G2133.origine: The Greek word comes from "eu" (good) and "nous" (mind, thought): it literally means "good thought" or "good inclination" towards someone. It describes that inner state where the will aligns with the action, without resistance or bitterness.
G2133.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament. In 1 Corinthians 7:3, it characterizes the marital relationship: husband and wife should serve one another not out of dry duty, but with goodwill. In Ephesians 6:7, it describes the attitude that slaves should adopt towards their masters: not forced obedience, but joyful service, as if rendered to the Lord. In both cases, Paul teaches that human relationships — whether marital or based on authority — should be marked by this sincere and enthusiastic disposition of the heart, not by mechanical obedience.
G2133.portee: This word reminds Christians that obedience and service are truly pleasing to God only if they spring from the heart. Whether one is a husband, wife, employee, or servant, doing something out of bitter obligation honors no one; but doing it with goodwill transforms it into a living offering. It is a call to serve — in marriage, work, the Church — not grumbling, but freely and wholeheartedly.

sens: To be castrated, deprived of virility by a physical intervention
Figuratively, to voluntarily abstain from marital relations or marriage to dedicate oneself to God
G2134.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to be made a eunuch, that is, to be castrated. This happens to some men in the royal courts of the ancient East, or to war captives. Jesus speaks of this in Matthew 19:12, distinguishing those who "have been made so by men," meaning those who have undergone this mutilation.

2. But Jesus also uses the verb figuratively when He says, "there are eunuchs who have made themselves so for the sake of the kingdom of heaven." Here, "to become a eunuch" means to freely choose to renounce marriage and fatherhood, not by violence or constraint, but by a personal act, to better serve God. It is a voluntary continence, accepted for the Kingdom.
G2134.origine: The word comes from the Greek εὐνοῦχος (eunouchos), which designates a eunuch. The verb εὐνουχίζω is its verbal form, literally meaning "to make a eunuch." The etymology of the word eunouchos is debated, but it historically designates a castrated man, a well-known reality in the ancient Near Eastern and Hellenistic empires. The verb here expresses both the action of castration and, metaphorically, that of self-renunciation.
G2134.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 19:12, where Jesus responds to His disciples about the question of marriage. He lists three categories of men who do not marry: those born so, those made eunuchs by others, and those who have made themselves eunuchs. In this context, Jesus validates the choice to remain single and continent, not as an obligation, but as a particular charism for some, granted "for the sake of the kingdom of heaven." It is a rare, concise word that recognizes voluntary continence as a gift from God.
G2134.portee: This word teaches that marriage is not a universal command in the Kingdom of God. It honors the choice to dedicate one's entire life to the service of God without the bonds of marriage, as many apostles and saints would later do. It invites each Christian to discern their own calling: marriage or continence. It is a word of freedom, not constraint; it values the personal decision made "for the sake of the kingdom of heaven."

sens: a castrated man, deprived of virility
a high dignitary at the court of a king or queen
one who voluntarily renounces marriage to serve God
G2135.detail:
1. A eunuch is literally a man who has undergone castration: he is a man without biological virility. In antiquity, this condition was imposed on slaves or captives, particularly so they could serve safely alongside the women of royal palaces. The Ethiopian encountered by Philip in Acts 8:27 belongs to this category.
2. The term also designates a political function: a eunuch is often a minister or high-ranking steward at court, with access to the king's secrets. The eunuch in Acts 8:27-28 is the treasurer of the queen of Ethiopia, which shows his position of influence and trust.
3. Figuratively, eunuch describes one who freely chooses not to marry in order to dedicate himself entirely to the service of God and the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 19:12). Jesus speaks of those who "have made themselves so" — not by castration, but by voluntary renunciation of marriage.
G2135.origine: The Greek word "eunouchos" literally comes from two Greek words: "eunè" (bed) and "echein" (to have, to keep) — it is one who "keeps the bed" or "watches over the bed," reflecting the primary function of eunuchs in ancient palaces. The Greek Old Testament translates the Hebrew word "saris" with this term, which referred both to a castrated servant and a high-ranking official. The underlying Hebrew word was often less specific than one might think: it could simply designate a steward or officer, not necessarily a castrated one.
G2135.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, all occurrences found in Matthew and Acts. In Matthew 19:12, Jesus uses it three times to speak of three types of eunuchs: those born so, those made so by men, and those who make themselves so for the kingdom. In Acts 8, the word designates the Ethiopian official whom Philip meets on the road: he is a historical figure of high rank, minister to Queen Candace, who came to worship in Jerusalem. The meaning thus shifts between the concrete (physical state or functional position) and the figurative (voluntary renunciation), depending on the context.
G2135.portee: For the Christian, this word invites reflection on renunciation and consecration.
