Jesus does not impose celibacy, but honors it as a free choice for the kingdom of God — a form of sacrifice accepted by those who have the vocation. The story of the Ethiopian eunuch also shows that social and religious barriers fall before grace: a man excluded from the Jewish temple by his condition becomes a baptized believer, welcomed into the family of God. It is a call to see beyond appearances and the statuses of the world.

sens: Christian woman from the church of Philippi
G2136.detail: Euodia is a Christian woman member of the assembly at Philippi. The Apostle Paul urges her, along with her companion Syntyche, to live in harmony "with the same mind in the Lord" (Philippians 4:2), suggesting that there was tension or disagreement between them in the local church.
G2136.origine: The name Euodia comes from Greek and literally means "good path" or "prosperity" (from eu, "good," and hodos, "path"). It is a compound name that expresses a wish for blessing, common in the Greek world of the time.
G2136.emploi: Euodia appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 4:2. She is mentioned alongside Syntyche, another important member of the church at Philippi. Paul mentions them among those "who have contended for the Gospel" (Philippians 4:3), showing that they played an active role in the proclamation of the faith. The fact that Paul addresses her by name testifies to her influence and importance in the local Christian community.

sens: To succeed in a journey or movement
To advance without obstacles, to progress favorably
To succeed, to flourish, to have success in one's endeavors
To enjoy good health or physical and moral well-being
G2137.detail:
1. The literal sense first evokes a journey that goes well: having a good path ahead, advancing smoothly toward one's destination. Paul prays that his desire "to come to you" may finally be fulfilled (Romans 1:10), where the word expresses this wish for a happy journey.
2. The word then extends to the general success of an endeavor: to progress, to advance without obstacles. In 1 Corinthians 16:2, he speaks of the gifts that each one will set aside "according to his prosperity," meaning according to what his affairs allow.
3. From there, it means to prosper in the broadest sense: to enjoy success, flourishing, blessing. John wishes for his friend to prosper "in all respects," meaning to succeed in all things (3 John 1:2).
4. In this same verse, "prosper" in the state of your soul evokes spiritual and moral health: when the soul is well, all is well — it is an inner prosperity that reflects God's protection and favor.
G2137.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek ὁδός ("way, path"), prefixed by εὖ ("well"). Literally, "to walk well." The root evokes the very concrete image of one who walks unobstructed on a good path. The Hebrew verb צָלַח ("to succeed, to prosper") in the Greek Old Testament captures this same idea: to advance, to succeed, to arrive safely, whether physically or in one's affairs. The basic image is that of a traveler or passerby who progresses well.
G2137.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in a context of blessing or wish. In Romans 1:10, Paul implores God to prosper him in his desire to go to Rome — it is a path made possible by God. In 1 Corinthians 16:2, the word takes on a material and economic sense: the prosperity that each one has from his goods. In 3 John 1:2, John addresses Gaius with a triple wish: that all may prosper for him, that he may be in good health, and that his soul may prosper as well. In all cases, the word expresses a life placed under God's blessing and favorable guidance.
G2137.portee: This word invites the believer to see that prosperity is not primarily an accumulation of wealth, but a journey made possible by God: one who walks without obstacles, who does not stumble against walls, who advances toward legitimate goals with divine favor. The soul that prospers (3 John 1:2) is a soul that God accompanies and blesses from within. For Paul, even the simple desire to visit a church far from him depends on this prosperity given by God.

sens: One who is willing to obey, to yield
One who can be persuaded
One who seeks agreement rather than conflict
G2138.detail:
1. The word describes one who is ready to obey, to follow the directives or advice of others without resistance. It is an ability to submit voluntarily, not out of weakness, but out of wisdom. In James 3:17, the wisdom that comes from above is described as "conciliatory," meaning it does not impose its will rigidly, but remains open and receptive.

2. The word also evokes one who can be persuaded by just reasons, who welcomes good words and wise counsel. It is a form of positive docility: not naivety or servility, but the ability to recognize the truth when encountered.

3. More broadly, it is a disposition to seek peace and understanding rather than confrontation or domination. Conciliatory wisdom prefers harmony and dialogue to the clash of wills.
G2138.origine: The Greek word combines εὖ (well, good) and πείθομαι (to be persuaded, to obey). It literally designates one in whom resides "good obedience" or "being well persuaded." The root πείθ- evokes the action of convincing and obtaining assent. It is a compound that emphasizes a positive quality: it is not merely passive obedience, but a disposition of the heart to welcome truth and wisdom.
G2138.emploi: The word appears only once in James in James 3:17, in the description of the characteristic traits of "the wisdom from above." Situated in a list of spiritual qualities (purity, peace, moderation, mercy, good fruits), the quality of being conciliatory is presented as closely related to the absence of duplicity and hypocrisy. It belongs to the sphere of Christian virtues and describes how true divine wisdom manifests in relationships and decisions: with flexibility, listening, and a sincere desire for agreement rather than personal victory.
G2138.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that true wisdom is never rigid or authoritarian: it combines firmness in principles and flexibility in relationships. To be conciliatory, in the biblical sense, is not to renounce the truth, but to serve it with humility and gentleness. It is a call to cultivate a disposition of the heart that listens, weighs, and adjusts, reflecting the divine wisdom that alone can guide us toward true peace.

sens: What hinders us, weighs us down, and slows us in the race
The sin that clings so easily to us and chains us
What surrounds us, envelops us, and suffocates us
G2139.detail:
1. The word first designates what weighs on us, which burdens us and prevents us from moving freely — like a burden we carry on our shoulders. In Hebrews 12:1, the apostle invites believers to throw off what slows them down, like a runner who sheds heavy clothing before the race.
2. It then applies to the sins that surround us and cling to us, which constantly weigh us down: these are not just external obstacles, but chains that we drag along with us. The biblical context shows that these sins are easy to contract and difficult to shake off.
3. The word finally evokes the image of being surrounded, enveloped, encircled on all sides — like someone struggling in a net. It is the idea of an oppressive presence that encircles and suffocates us, hence the importance of rejecting it to run freely.
G2139.origine: The Greek word is composed of three elements: "eu" (well), "peri" (around), and "histèmi" (to stand, to place). The proper sense was "well placed around," "which stands easily around us." Over time, it took on the meaning of "that easily envelops us," "that encircles us without difficulty." Its first biblical usage shows that it describes the sins that closely surround us and easily encircle us, like an atmosphere from which we cannot escape.
G2139.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: in Hebrews 12:1. The author uses it to exhort believers to reject "every burden and the sin that so easily ensnares us." The context is that of a long-distance race, of perseverance in faith despite obstacles. The burden in question is not just sin in general, but that which particularly clings to us, which encircles us and slows us down at every step. It is a rare and chosen word for its imagery power.
G2139.portee: This word teaches us that the Christian life is a race, and that certain sins are special hindrances — those that return constantly, that closely surround us, that cling to our skin. The text calls us to recognize them and to shed them with determination, rather than dragging them indefinitely. It is an invitation to the freedom and lightness of faith, not the absence of all suffering, but the refusal of what unnecessarily chains us.

sens: Action of doing good to others
Active and concrete generosity towards those in need
Gift or beneficial act granted to someone
G2140.detail:
1. Benevolence is the action of doing good, showing kindness to others. It is a positive, voluntary act that seeks to relieve or help. In Hebrews 13:16, the apostle invites believers not to forget benevolence: it is part of what God calls a true sacrifice, more precious than the old offerings.
2. Benevolence is a practical generosity that is shown through concrete gestures — giving, sharing, materially helping. It aligns with the "liberality" mentioned in the same verse: it is giving of oneself, of one's possessions, without expecting anything in return.
3. Benevolence can also refer to a benefit received, an act of grace granted to the one who receives it. This meaning emphasizes that doing good to someone is to confer upon them a gift, a favor.
G2140.origine: The Greek word comes from the root "eu" (good) and "poiia" (action of doing, producing). It literally means "doing good." In Greek, the family includes words for "good" and for "doing": it is an active term that emphasizes the production of good, not a passive disposition. This word often translates in the Greek Old Testament terms related to mercy and acts of assistance towards the poor.
G2140.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 13:16, in a final exhortation. The apostle places benevolence and liberality at the heart of what God honors: they are not secondary acts, but sacrifices — offerings of the heart — that God "takes pleasure" in. It is a noble, almost solemn term that shows that kindness towards others carries spiritual dignity.
G2140.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that faith without works of charity is empty. Benevolence is not an optional supplement, but a central element of the Christian life that is pleasing to God. It calls for a transition from good intention to concrete action: sharing, giving, helping those who suffer, for that is where God delights.

sens: Having financial resources, wealth
Being able to do something thanks to these resources
Enjoying comfort, prosperity
G2141.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to having money, goods, resources at one's disposal. In Acts 11:29, the disciples "according to their means" send aid: each gives what they possess and can afford to give.
2. More broadly, it means being able, having the capacity to do something — not just the will, but the concrete resources to accomplish it. Having means means being able to act.
3. The word also evokes the state of one who prospers, who lives in comfort and lacks nothing. It is enjoying a stable and sufficient material life.
G2141.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek "eu" (good) and "poros" (passage, resource, means). The basic image is that of an open path, a possible passage: one who has means has a clear way to act. The word thus expresses both the idea of wealth and the capacity for action. In the Greek of the Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew "nasag" in the sense of "to be able to, to be able to reach."
G2141.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 11:29. It describes the attitude of the Christian disciples of Antioch in the face of a famine threatening Judea: they decide to send aid according to their means to the brothers in distress. The context shows that the word applies here to real material resources and the concrete capacity to help. It is a rare but telling term: the Bible uses it to express that Christian help should be measured by what each actually possesses, not by what they do not possess.
G2141.portee: This word reminds us of a simple and important truth for Christian life: God does not ask for the impossible. When we give, we give according to our means — that is the fair and reasonable measure. This prohibits both selfish greed and unrealistic demands. It is a call to lucid and responsible generosity, one that recognizes both the need of the brother and the reality of what one possesses.

sens: material comfort, prosperity
ease, absence of hindrance
G2142.detail:
1. Well-being refers to material comfort, prosperity — the state of one who enjoys sufficient resources and lives without lack. Demetrius the silversmith, fearing that Paul's preaching would ruin his business, reminds his fellow craftsmen that "our well-being depends on this industry" (Acts 19:25): he speaks of their common prosperity, threatened by the conversion of customers. It is the comfort and wealth that allow for an easy life.
2. The word can also refer to ease, the absence of obstacles — the state of one who finds everything within reach. This nuance was known to the ancient Greek translators of the Old Testament.
G2142.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to be able, to have means," with the prefix "eu-" (good). It is formed as a compound: it literally describes the state of one who "walks well" or "manages their affairs well." In ancient Greek, the word applied to economic prosperity and material comfort.
G2142.emploi: This term appears only once in the New Testament: in Acts 19:25. It is Demetrius, a silversmith from Ephesus, who uses it when addressing his fellow craftsmen. The context is that of Paul's preaching, which has led many Ephesians to reject idolatry and cease buying the small shrines of Artemis that these craftsmen made. Demetrius then mentions "well-being" in their profession — a prosperity that the Christian mission directly threatens.
G2142.portee: This word reminds us of a constant temptation: the selfish defense of our material interests in the face of the Gospel. Demetrius embodies one who, seeing faith in Jesus Christ challenge his lucrative business, chooses to combat the Good News out of economic interest. For the believer, it is a warning: not to let the pursuit of temporal well-being distance us from or oppose the will of God.

sens: The pleasant and attractive appearance of the body or of a thing
The brilliance of what is beautiful, what pleases the eye
The external aspect and its ephemeral splendor
G2143.detail:
1. Beauty is the pleasant appearance that pleases the eye: what is well-formed, harmonious, attractive. In James 1:11, it is the beauty of the flower of the grass, its delicate and radiant appearance that captures attention.
2. The word emphasizes the visible brilliance, the splendor that emanates from what is beautiful: it is the impression one receives upon seeing it. The flower of the grass possesses this brilliance that fades as soon as the sun dries it up.
3. James uses this word to evoke something beautiful yet fragile and temporary: the external beauty that fades like the withered flower. This highlights the contrast with the internal and lasting beauty that God appreciates.
G2143.origine: The word comes from the root "eu" (good) and "prepia" (that which is suitable, that which is worthy). It literally designates what "fits well," what perfectly matches and produces a good impression. The same root is found in the word "preponderance" in French. This word accounts in the Greek Old Testament for the Hebrew word hadar, which means both honor, brilliance, and splendor.
G2143.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 1:11. The apostle James uses it in his illustration of the vanity of riches: just as the flower of the grass loses its beauty when the burning sun dries up the plant, the rich will wither in their enterprises. The context shows that James speaks of external and visible beauty, that which attracted the eye but quickly disappears, to teach us that all that is purely earthly and material loses its appeal and value.
G2143.portee: This word warns us against the illusion of believing that external beauty is lasting or essential. James calls us to look beyond the fleeting appearance of this world, including visible wealth and splendor. He invites us to seek true beauty, that which comes from God and endures: inner beauty, love, wisdom, and faith.

sens: That which pleases, is suitable, and is received with satisfaction
That which is accepted, approved by someone
That which is timely, that comes at the right moment
G2144.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is that of what pleases and satisfies the one who receives it. It is the positive acceptance of an offering or a person. In 1 Peter 2:5, spiritual sacrifices are pleasing to God, meaning they please Him and He receives them favorably.
2. The word also describes what is approved and accepted by someone in authority. In Romans 15:31, Paul wishes that the gifts he brings to Jerusalem be accepted (approved, received with kindness) by the saints.
3. A more temporal sense: what happens at the right moment, what is suitable for the time. In 2 Corinthians 6:2, the favorable time is the opportune moment when God listens and saves — the moment that is perfectly fitting.
G2144.origine: The Greek word comes from the combination of two elements: "eu" (well) and "prosdektos" (that which is received, accepted). The root "dechomai" means to receive or welcome. It is a strengthened form of the simpler adjective "dektos": "eu-prosdektos" emphasizes the particularly acceptable nature of what is received. The prefix "pro" adds the idea of an expectation, a reception that looks forward.
G2144.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and Peter. In Romans 15:16, Paul uses this term to describe how the Gentiles, sanctified by the Spirit, become a pleasing offering to God. In Romans 15:31, he uses it to request that his gifts be well received by the Christians in Jerusalem. In 2 Corinthians 6:2, it is in the context of the time of divine grace — the favorable moment of salvation. In 2 Corinthians 8:12, Paul emphasizes that the voluntary offering, even modest, is pleasing to God according to what each one has. In 1 Peter 2:5, believers offer spiritual sacrifices pleasing to God. The adjective thus carries both a cultic dimension (sacrifices, offerings) and a moral dimension (gifts, goodwill).
G2144.portee: This word reminds the believer that God favorably receives our offerings and actions if the heart is sincere and the spirit willing. It assures that our gifts, even modest, and our spiritual sacrifices (praise, service, generosity) are received and appreciated by the Father. It is a word of grace: we never offer in vain to God if we offer through Jesus Christ with a pure heart.

sens: To remain continually beside someone or something
To be entirely available to serve or honor
To be focused, without distraction
G2145.detail:
1. The word paints the image of one who remains seated at the feet or beside a person, in a constant and devoted presence. It is to be attached to someone without straying away.
2. In a spiritual context, it means to dedicate oneself entirely to someone or to a cause — here, to the Lord — by making available all one's heart and strength.
3. The word especially emphasizes the absence of distraction: one who is "attached" to the Lord does not divide their attention, nor allow themselves to be diverted by other concerns. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 7:35 to urge a devotion without distraction to the Lord, without being fragmented by the worries of the world.
G2145.origine: The word combines the prefix "eu-" (well, good) and a root meaning "to sit near" or "beside." The same image is found in the Hebrew word meaning "to remain seated beside." It is a common image in the New Testament to describe the disciple who sits at the feet of the master or who remains in his presence.
G2145.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 7:35. Paul uses it in a passage where he advises Christians on marriage and celibacy. He argues that celibacy allows for undistracted devotion to the Lord: one who is unmarried can be "attached" to the Lord, meaning entirely available to serve and honor Him. The context shows that Paul values this concentration of heart on Christ rather than the division of affections.
G2145.portee: This word reminds the Christian that true spiritual wealth is not in the diversity of occupations, but in the depth of attachment to the Lord. Being "attached" without distraction invites us to examine where our strengths, time, and attention truly go — a relevant invitation for anyone seeking to live fully for Christ.

sens: To have a good appearance, to present oneself well
To seek to please on the surface, to showcase one's image
To seek to charm or impose by appearance rather than by substance
G2146.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of having a good aspect, presenting oneself in an attractive way — the basic image comes from the Greek for "beautiful face." It is to make a good figure, to appear well in the eyes of others.
2. In the biblical context, it takes on a negative shade: seeking to please or impress by the outside, giving a flattering image of oneself. In Galatians 6:12, Paul criticizes those who want to "appear well according to the flesh" by imposing circumcision on converts, not out of love for the faith but to avoid persecution: they make a good figure in the eyes of the Jews.
3. The underlying idea is that this beautiful appearance hides a bad motivation or lack of sincerity. It is to seek human approval rather than that of God.
G2146.origine: The word is composed of "eu" (well) and "prosopon" (face, appearance). The image is that of a beautiful or impressive face. This compound expresses the general idea of making a good figure, showing oneself in a good light — naturally on a physical level first, then figuratively on a moral or social level.
G2146.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 6:12. Paul uses it to describe the behavior of false teachers who seek to impose circumcision on believers of pagan origin. Their stated goal: "to make a good impression according to the flesh," that is, to please the Jewish authorities and thus avoid being persecuted for the cross of Christ. Paul contrasts the pursuit of human prestige with sincere attachment to the Gospel. The verb denounces religious hypocrisy and compromise for purely social reasons.
G2146.portee: This word challenges the Christian on their true motivations. Are we seeking to please God or man? Do we act out of conviction and love, or to look good and avoid criticism? Paul invites us to reject religious hypocrisy and compromise for prestige. Authentic faith does not need a beautiful appearance; it manifests through sincerity and love of the cross, even if it costs dearly.

sens: Discover something or someone after searching or along the way
Encounter a person by chance or unexpectedly
Observe the existence or state of something
Acquire, obtain, receive something
Discover, learn through investigation or reflection
In the passive: be discovered, revealed, disappear
G2147.detail:
1. Finding what one is looking for: after a quest, one discovers the object or person. Example: "A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard. He came seeking fruit on it, and found none" (Luke 13:6). The basic meaning is the success of a search.
2. Meeting someone unexpectedly, without having specifically sought them: "Philip found Nathanael and said to him: We have found him of whom Moses wrote" (John 1:45). This is a chance encounter or crossing of paths.
3. Observing a state, verifying the reality of a situation: "Mary, his mother, was betrothed to Joseph, and she was found with child of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 1:18). One discovers a fact, an established reality.
4. Obtaining, procuring something for oneself: "For whoever wants to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it" (Matthew 16:25). Here, finding means acquiring, possessing, receiving in exchange.
5. Discovering, learning through investigation or reasoning: "They found no crime worthy of death" (Luke 23:22). This is the result of an inquiry, a judgment.
6. In the passive: being discovered, revealed in the open, or disappearing from view: "Those who seek a pretext... may be found as we are" (2 Corinthians 11:12). The subject is exposed or characterized publicly.
G2147.origine: The word comes from classical Greek and originally meant "to arrive at, to reach." In biblical Greek, it primarily translates the Hebrew מצא (matsa), which has the same semantic field: to seek and to discover. This Hebrew root expresses the action of meeting, observing, possessing. Greek has retained this flexibility: the word can be used without a complement ("seek and you will find") or with an object ("find something"). The passivity of the verb in Greek also brings the idea of being discovered, revealed.
G2147.emploi: The verb "find" is one of the most frequent in the New Testament (167 occurrences). It appears mainly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and in Acts. Its meaning varies according to the context: active and rewarded search (Luke 11:9-10: "He who seeks finds"), chance discovery (meeting people), observation of a state of fact (notably in the passive to reveal), and acquisition or obtaining in a figurative sense (receiving grace, life). In the Passion narratives, the verb often refers to what is discovered through inquiry: "They found no crime to charge him with" (Luke 23:22, 23:4). This semantic richness reflects the flexibility of the term in common Greek and its fidelity to the Hebrew concept.
G2147.portee: The word "find" invites the reader to hope: to seek is to be able to find. God is not hidden from those who sincerely seek him (Acts 17:27). It also encourages gratitude for what is received unexpectedly, like grace. In Pauline theology, "being found in Christ" means being recognized as righteous by God (Philippians 3:9). It is a word of assurance for prayer and the life of faith: the spiritual quest does not remain barren; the hidden treasure in the field will be discovered by the one who seeks with all their heart.

sens: violent northeast wind
G2148.detail: 1. Violent northeast wind: the word designates a brutal wind blowing between the east and north, known to sailors of the ancient Mediterranean. Its very name reveals its character: it combines the name of the east wind (Eurus) and that of the north wind in Latin (Aquilo). In Acts 27:14, this wind suddenly strikes the island and threatens the ship carrying Paul to Italy.
G2148.origine: The word Euraquilon is a technical term from marine navigation, composed of two roots: Eurus (the east wind) from Greek and Aquilo (the north wind) from Latin. It is a hybrid Greco-Latin word, probably coined by the sailors themselves to designate this characteristic wind they were well acquainted with. Its existence in nautical vocabulary shows how the Greeks and Romans classified winds according to their directions.
G2148.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:14. Luke recounts Paul's journey to Rome: the ship is held not far from Cyprus when suddenly this northeast wind unleashes, violent and unexpected. The maritime context and the fact that Luke designates the wind by its technical name suggest that he has reliable sources for this shipwreck account, possibly an eyewitness. The wind becomes a hostile force threatening the sailors.
G2148.portee: This account reminds us that even an apostle and his companions can face unpredictable storms and real dangers. But later in the chapter, it is faith in God and obedience to his instructions that saves the lives of all the passengers. The raging wind thus becomes the backdrop where trust in God proves stronger than the unleashed forces of nature.

sens: Offering a lot of space, wide and extensive
Figuratively: easily welcoming, without restriction
G2149.detail:
1. The word primarily describes what is physically wide, ample, capable of containing much. In Matthew 7:13, Jesus speaks of the "spacious way" that leads to destruction — it is an image: this way imposes no limits, it is comfortable, easy to follow, without narrowness or constraint.
2. In a figurative sense, "spacious" characterizes what is open, permissive, without strict demands. The wide path of Matthew 7:13 symbolizes a life without moral discipline, one that many choose because it requires little renunciation and does not hinder anyone.
G2149.origine: The Greek word is formed from two elements: εὐρύς (euus, "wide") and χώρα (chōra, "place, space"). It belongs to the same family as several words describing extent or generosity. In Hebrew, it usually translates the root רָחַב (rahab, "to be wide"), which describes physical space or, figuratively, life without oppression.
G2149.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 7:13. Jesus uses it in his teaching about the two paths: the narrow path that leads to life, and the spacious path that leads to destruction. The opposition between "narrow" and "spacious" is not primarily a question of physicality, but of morality and spiritual choice. Many prefer the spacious path because it demands no sacrifice.
G2149.portee: This word invites reflection on the real cost of Christian discipleship. The spacious path seems attractive because it costs nothing; the narrow path requires renunciation and vigilance. Jesus reminds us that ease is not a sign of truth, and that what pleases the majority is not always what leads to true life. It is a call to choose consciously, against the current.

sens: respect for parents and superiors
reverence for God
practical obedience to God's commandments
life in accordance with God's will
G2150.detail:
1. Piety begins with respect: it is primarily the attitude of reverence owed to those who have raised us or who govern us — a form of recognition and submission (Acts 3:12).
2. However, true piety is primarily directed towards God: it is that respectful fear and love that lead us to serve and obey Him. Paul calls this "the mystery of piety" (1 Timothy 3:16).
3. Piety is not a mere emotion: it is lived out, practiced, and trained like a discipline. Paul advises Timothy: "Train yourself in piety" (1 Timothy 4:8), for it carries with it a promise, that of a good life here and eternal life.
4. It is a life that seeks righteousness, faith, love (1 Timothy 6:11) and allows itself to be transformed by the knowledge of God according to the truth (Titus 1:1). It is never a facade: a mere appearance of piety without real strength (2 Timothy 3:5) is meaningless.
G2150.origine: The Greek word comes from "eu" (good) and "sebeia" (reverence, worship). Literally, it is a "good reverence." It often translates the Hebrew "yirah" (fear) in the Greek Old Testament, particularly the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom. This root evokes the image of a person respectfully bowing before the one they honor — a bodily attitude that reflects a posture of the soul.
G2150.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the letters of Paul and Peter addressed to Christian communities. It denotes the true religious life of the believer. Paul speaks of it as a reality to be actively cultivated (1 Timothy 4:8), a spiritual training that grants access to present and future goods. But he also warns against the false pious, those who have the appearance of piety without its reality (2 Timothy 3:5), or those who turn it into a lucrative business (1 Timothy 6:5). In Peter's writings, piety is linked to spiritual growth: it is added to faith and virtue (2 Peter 1:6-7). It is a church word that exposes what it means to live as a child of God.
G2150.portee: For the Christian, this word invites us to take religious life seriously, not as mere external conformity but as a living relationship with God that transforms everything we do. Piety is not an ornament or an appearance: it is a discipline, a regular training that nourishes the soul and prepares it for glory. It also warns us against the lie of believing that we can have God without change: true piety is always visible in righteousness, love, and faithfulness.

sens: To show religious respect towards someone or something
To fulfill with dedication a family duty or moral commitment
G2151.detail:
1. To revere is to show respect towards God or towards what one considers sacred. It is to recognize something or someone as worthy of honor and veneration. In Athens, Paul tells the inhabitants that they revere an altar dedicated "to an unknown god" (Acts 17:23): they perform a religious act, even if they do not truly know the object of their worship.
2. To fulfill a duty of piety towards someone — of respectful and responsible love. When one exercises this piety towards their family, they show that they cherish and care for them in a conscious and committed way. In 1 Timothy 5:4, the children of a widow must "exercise piety" towards their parents: it is to honor and tenderly fulfill the obligations received from them.
G2151.origine: The word comes from εὐ- (well) and σέβομαι (to revere, to respect). It thus means "to well-revere" or "to show pious respect." The adjective εὐσεβής (pious, devout) describes one who honors God or their duties with respectful fear. This family of words always expresses an attitude of sacred respect, rooted in the awareness of standing before something or someone greater than oneself.
G2151.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Athens (Acts 17:23), Paul uses it to describe the religious act of the Athenians towards their altars, a fear or respect for the divine that seeks its object. In 1 Timothy 5:4, the context is familial and moral: it is to honor one's parents by supporting them materially and emotionally. In both cases, the word denotes a serious, conscious attitude that implies recognizing an obligation and fulfilling it with awareness.
G2151.portee: This word reminds us that authentic piety is not limited to empty gestures: it is to recognize what deserves our respect — first God, and then also those who gave us life. It invites us to examine what we truly revere and to manifest our reverence not through words, but through concrete and faithful actions, particularly towards our family.

sens: Who fears God and respects Him deeply
Who lives according to God's commandments with dedication
Who honors God through their actions and attitude
G2152.detail:
1. The word primarily describes an inner attitude: a sincere reverence towards God, a respectful fear that arises from the conviction that God is holy and worthy of worship. Cornelius, in Acts 10:2, is described as "pious" — he is a man who "fears God" with all his heart, the first trait that characterizes him.
2. This piety is then manifested in concrete life: the one who is pious acts justly, does good, obeys God's laws. Cornelius does not pray in secret only; he "does many alms" (Acts 10:2), and even his military servant is said to be "pious," showing that virtue is recognized through actions.
3. Finally, in 2 Peter 2:9, the Lord "knows how to deliver the pious from trial": piety is a living relationship with God that receives His protection and help, especially on the day of judgment. It is a quality that God recognizes and rewards.
G2152.origine: The Greek word "pious" comes from two roots: "good" (eu) and "to revere" or "to fear" (sebô), literally "to well-fear." It thus describes one who maintains a healthy fear of God, not a paralyzing fear but a loving respect. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates "just" (tsaddîq in Hebrew, in Proverbs and Isaiah) or "pious" (hasîd), showing that biblical piety and justice go together: it is to live in harmony with God's will.
G2152.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. It first describes Cornelius, a Roman officer who fears God and lives in accordance with his moral conscience (Acts 10:2, 10:7) — a non-Jew whom God recognizes as pious. He is a key figure: his conversion marks the opening of the Gospel to the Gentiles. Then, in 2 Peter 2:9, the term characterizes all believers whom the Lord protects amid trials, in contrast to "the unjust" who await judgment. The emphasis is always on a piety that unites fear of God, practical obedience, and expectation of His justice.
G2152.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites us to consider what it truly means to fear God: not a terror, but a reverence that directs all actions towards Him. Cornelius shows that authentic piety is recognized by its fruits (almsgiving, prayer) and that it attracts the attention of God Himself. It is also an assurance: God "knows how to deliver the pious from trial," a word of security for all those who seek to live in His presence.

sens: With respect and fear towards God
In a manner faithful to religion and God's commandments
With a moral and holy life
G2153.detail:
1. The word first evokes an inner attitude: the one who acts piously recognizes God as his Lord and fears Him with respect. It is a sincere piety, aware of God's presence. In 2 Timothy 3:12, Paul speaks of those "who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus," showing that piety is a deliberate choice, a commitment to honor God through daily life.
2. To live piously also means to live according to God's rules and commandments, in accordance with His will. It is not a vague feeling, but a concrete conduct. In Titus 2:12, the apostle links piety to renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, then to a wise and righteous life: piety is measured by actions, behavior, and daily choices.
G2153.origine: The word comes from the Greek root "eu" (well) and "sebein" (to respect, to fear). The adverb "piously" literally denotes a good fear, a respectful fear. In ancient Greek, the word translates the Hebrew "yirah" (fear of God) which expresses not fear, but respect and reverence towards the Most High. It is a deep spiritual attitude: recognizing God's holiness and desiring to please Him.
G2153.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In 2 Timothy 3:12, it describes the lifestyle of the authentic believer: "to live piously in Christ Jesus" announces persecution, for true piety conflicts with the values of the world. In Titus 2:12, it qualifies practical wisdom: "to live piously" means to renounce fleshly passions and adopt a righteous and sensible conduct. Both passages show that piety is not an isolated feeling, but a general orientation of life towards God and good.
G2153.portee: This word invites the reader to take seriously the stakes of his life: to live piously is not a secondary option, but the heart of the Christian path. It is a call to transform one's daily conduct through respect for God and obedience to His word. But this path requires courage: as 2 Timothy 3:12 announces, true piety is not pleasing to the world and may attract opposition. However, it alone offers the believer a life in accordance with divine wisdom and justice.

sens: Easy to see, to notice, clearly stands out
Easy to understand, clear to the mind
G2154.detail:
1. The word first designates what is visible and manifest, which clearly stands out from the rest — like a sign that is easily seen. It conveys the idea of something that appears clearly to the eyes or attention.
2. Figuratively, it describes what is understandable, clear to the intellect. In 1 Corinthians 14:9, Paul uses it to say that a word must be "distinct," meaning clear and intelligible: if you speak in a language that no one understands, your words remain confused and vain, you "speak into the air." The word thus emphasizes the clarity of the message that reaches the mind of the listener.
G2154.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "well" (εὖ) associated with the idea of sign or signal. This combination expresses what is a good sign, easy to recognize and interpret. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates a Hebrew word (כֶּסֶא) evoking clarity or visibility. The family of the word carries the general idea of a manifest and intelligible sign.
G2154.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 14:9. Paul uses it in his teaching on spiritual gifts, particularly speaking in tongues. He emphasizes the importance that the word be "distinct," that is, understandable for the listeners. In this context, the clarity of the message is paramount: a word without clarity, even spiritual, does not build up the assembly.
G2154.portee: This word reminds Christians of a crucial truth: true love is expressed through clarity and intelligibility. When speaking in the assembly, it is not enough to have a message; that message must be clear so that everyone receives it and is edified. It is an exhortation to the responsibility of the speaker: to serve others through clear and accessible communication.

sens: Having sensitive entrails, a tender heart
Experiencing compassion, pity towards others
Manifesting this tenderness in behavior and words
G2155.detail: 1. The word literally evokes a deep sensitivity of the heart: the one who is compassionate is not closed off or insensitive, but his innards are stirred by the suffering of others — it is an inner disposition of feeling. 2. This sensitivity produces compassion, that is, the ability to share in another's pain and take it to heart, as shown by the call to be "full of compassion" alongside brotherly love in 1 Peter 3:8. 3. The compassionate does not remain locked in his feelings: he acts, he forgives, he treats others with kindness. This is what Ephesians 4:32 teaches, where being compassionate means forgiving one another, letting the tenderness of the heart guide reconciliation.
G2155.origine: The Greek word is composed of εὖ (well, good) and σπλάγχνον (entrails, heart, seat of emotions). In ancient Greek, the entrails do not denote anatomy alone, but the center of deep feelings, compassion, and affection. This image aligns with the Hebrew חמל (to have pity) and related roots that express this visceral tenderness of the heart towards the suffering one.
G2155.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two cited places: Ephesians and 1 Peter. Each time, it is part of an exhortation to the fraternal life of the Church. In Ephesians 4:32, compassion is concretely manifested in mutual forgiveness — forgiving as God forgave in Christ, with the sensitivity of the heart that means one does not forgive coldly but with affection. In 1 Peter 3:8, being compassionate is presented as a major virtue of the Christian community, alongside brotherly love and humility. These two passages show that compassion is not a weakness, but an essential moral and spiritual strength for communal life.
G2155.portee: For the Christian reader, this word calls to examine his heart: am I closed off or tender in the face of another's suffering? Compassion is presented as the beating heart of Christian brotherhood: without it, forgiveness remains formal, and the community disintegrates. Cultivating a compassionate heart is to reflect the very compassion of Christ and honor the forgiveness He has granted us.

sens: in a worthy, suitable manner that inspires respect
in an orderly and decent manner, conforming to good morals
in a way that preserves one's honor and reputation
G2156.detail: 1. The word describes a way of acting that is worthy and suitable, deserving of esteem. Let us walk "honestly, as in the day" (Romans 13:13): this means living in such a way that there is nothing to hide, that one can be seen in broad daylight without shame. 2. It also means to act with order and decency, respecting conventions. "Let all things be done decently and in order" (1 Corinthians 14:40) means that actions, even spiritual ones, must take place in an organized and respectable manner, not in disorder or indecency. 3. Finally, it is to conduct oneself in such a way as to maintain one's honor before all. "You should conduct yourselves honestly toward those outside" (1 Thessalonians 4:12): even in the presence of non-believers, one acts in a way that does not tarnish the name of Christ through a bad reputation.
G2156.origine: The Greek word comes from "euschēmōn" which literally means "of good form, well-formed." It is composed of "eu" (well) and "schēma" (form, appearance, shape). The original idea is that of a person or action that has a beautiful appearance, that is worthy and suitable. This is why the word extends to any conduct that has this quality of respect and decency.
G2156.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in relation to the moral conduct of the Christian. In Romans 13:13, Paul calls for walking "honestly" by fleeing drunkenness and lust — it is the conduct of the day, not of the night. In 1 Corinthians 14:40, he emphasizes order and decency in gatherings; "honestly" here opposes chaos and lack of spiritual restraint. In 1 Thessalonians 4:12, he encourages believers to conduct themselves "honestly" before those outside, showing that the Christian testimony also involves respecting appropriate social norms. In all cases, it is a virtue of ordinary life, not a spiritual extravagance.
G2156.portee: For the Christian, this exhortation reminds us that the gospel does not deprive us of a sense of honor and respect. Our faith must be expressed in a worthy, orderly, and respectable conduct — not hypocritical, but simply honest and faithful. It is through this "honesty" in small things that we testify to others of the power of Christ and maintain a good conscience.

sens: Quality of what is decent, suitable, worthy of respect
Decency of the body, modesty in attire and appearance
G2157.detail:
1. The word designates what is in accordance with conventions, what deserves respect and honor by its appearance or presentation. It is the quality of what is presentable, worthy, suitable in the eyes of others. In 1 Corinthians 12:23, Paul uses it to describe the members of the body that seem less noble or less worthy: these, he says, receive "more honesty," meaning they are treated with more care and respect, they are covered more.
2. Concretely, this evokes modesty and decency of the body — the idea that there are parts that are not naturally shown, and that are adorned with more clothing or care. Paul uses this image to teach that in the Church, the body of Christ, the members that appear to be the weakest or least honorable deserve indeed more attention and dignity.
G2157.origine: The word comes from two Greek elements: "eu-" (well) and "schèma" (form, appearance). It literally designates a "beautiful form" or a "good appearance." The root "schèma" evokes what is visible, the external presentation. The word belongs to the family of "euschēmōn" (decent, of good appearance), which appears in the New Testament to describe what is worthy and respectable.
G2157.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 12:23. Paul uses it in his teaching on the unity of the body of Christ: he explains that the members of the body that seem the least honorable receive "more honesty," meaning they are given more care, more clothing, more protection. It is an image of the respect and attention that Christians should give to those who appear weak or insignificant.
G2157.portee: This word invites the reader to reconsider their hierarchy of values: what seems weak or unworthy in the eyes of the world actually deserves more care and respect. It teaches that in the Church, there are no members without value, and that true honor consists in valuing the most fragile or hidden, just as Jesus did when he washed the feet of his disciples.

sens: Having an elegant, graceful, suitable appearance
Enjoying prestige, high social rank, influence
Morally suitable, decent, worthy
G2158.detail:
1. The word first describes what pleases the eye by its form or appearance: something elegant and graceful. In 1 Corinthians 12:24, Paul speaks of the "honorable members" of the human body, those who have a beautiful natural appearance and do not need clothing to be presentable. This is the primary image of the word: beautiful form.

2. In the social context, the word designates someone who occupies a position of prestige and influence, often related to wealth or status. When Mark 15:43 speaks of Joseph of Arimathea as a "distinguished counselor," it refers to a respected man of high rank; similarly, in Acts 13:50 and 17:12, the "distinguished women" are women of high social standing, probably wealthy and influential, whose social weight can be used to persecute or to welcome the message.

3. The word can also qualify what is morally suitable or decent, what befits dignity: in 1 Corinthians 7:35, Paul wants to lead believers to what is "decent," that is, what is fitting before God, without distraction.
G2158.origine: The word is composed of "eu" (well) and "schêma" (form, appearance). It literally designates what has a good form, a beautiful appearance. The root evokes the idea of external form, of what is seen and shown. It is a classical Greek word that has retained this sense of suitability and social prestige.
G2158.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament. Mark and Acts mainly use it to qualify people of high social rank or wealth (Joseph of Arimathea, the influential women of the cities). Paul also uses it in 1 Corinthians with two nuances: in 12:24, he speaks of the parts of the body that naturally have a beautiful appearance; in 7:35, he uses it in a moral sense, to designate what is fitting, what befits Christian life. The word thus oscillates between the social sense (having prestige, being influential) and the moral sense (being worthy, suitable).
G2158.portee: This word reminds us that God looks beyond appearances and social prestige. Joseph of Arimathea is described as a "distinguished" man, but what truly defines him is that he "was also waiting for the kingdom of God" and that he dared to honor Jesus at the risk of his reputation. The "distinguished women" in Acts listened to the Gospel and believed: their social rank did not close their hearts. Paul reminds the Corinthians that what is truly "decent" is not what the world values, but what honors God and builds up the body of Christ.

sens: with force and vigor
with intensity and fervor
with great conviction or determination
G2159.detail:
1. The word describes an action carried out with physical or energetic force, marked vigor. In Luke 23:10, the chief priests and scribes accuse Jesus "violently," meaning with brutal and passionate force.
2. It denotes ardor, emotional or verbal intensity in action. In Acts 18:28, Apollos "vigorously refutes" the Jews: he does not merely engage in polite discussion, but argues with strong conviction and marked zeal.
3. By extension, it characterizes a word or action carried out with authority and determination, without weakness or hesitation.
G2159.origine: The word comes from the Greek root "eu" (well, good) and "teinô" (to stretch, to extend), hence the image of a "good tension." It literally expresses what has tone, muscular or moral strength. It is an adverb, meaning it modifies an action or state to indicate the energetic manner in which it is performed.
G2159.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 23:10, during Jesus' trial, it depicts the determination of the religious authorities to condemn him: they do not merely accuse him, they do so "violently." In Acts 18:28, it characterizes Apollos' preaching: he is a man who defends Christianity "vigorously," with strength and conviction, putting all his energy into convincing his opponents through the power of the Scriptures. In both cases, the word emphasizes intensity and a lack of timidity.
G2159.portee: This word reminds the believer that faith in Christ requires not a weak adherence, but a vigorous commitment. Apollos, who "vigorously refutes" objections against Jesus, shows how Christian conviction should be expressed with fervor and clarity. For the reader, it is an invitation not to fear defending their faith with strength and persuasion.

sens: Witty or clever remark, agility of mind in conversation
Trivial, coarse joke that lacks respect and modesty
Inappropriate word, language that offends propriety and piety
G2160.detail:
1. Originally, the word denotes a kind of verbal agility or quick wit — the ability to bounce back gracefully on others' words. It is a valued social gift, the art of lively conversation.
2. However, this quickness of mind can degenerate into malicious mockery or hurtful jest. It then becomes a harsh word that ridicules or wounds.
3. The biblical sense emphasizes vulgar and coarse joking: that which mocks modesty or holiness. In Ephesians 5:4, Paul forbids it in the Christian's life, who should instead practice propriety and give thanks.
G2160.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: "eu" (well) and "trepo" (to turn, to twist). The image is of someone who "turns well" their words — who has a quick comeback. But by sliding into trivial joking, this "well turning" becomes a misuse of language. Paul uses it alongside related terms like foolish talk (μωρολογία) to describe language that is not fitting for the redeemed Christian.
G2160.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 5:4. Paul lists there the words that the believer must banish from their speech: dishonesty, foolish talk, and dishonest jest. Context: the apostle calls the Ephesians to walk worthy of the Gospel, where every word reflects holiness. Dishonest jest stands in opposition to the recognition and thanksgiving that a redeemed heart should express. It is an act of vigilance over the use of the tongue.
G2160.portee: This word reminds us that our speech reveals the state of our heart and our respect for God and others. Even humor, entertainment, and lightness of language should not slip into triviality or coarseness. It is a call to purity of language, a sign of a life transformed by the Gospel. The Christian should seek true joy, one that arises from gratitude, not from mockery that degrades.

sens: young man from Troas who fell asleep during Paul's preaching
G2161.detail: Eutychus is a young man living in Troas, a city on the northeast coast of Asia Minor. During a church meeting, while Paul preaches for a long time in a third-floor room, Eutychus, sitting in the window, falls asleep and falls from the building; he dies from the fall. Paul goes down, lays on the young man, and cries that life has returned to him.
G2161.origine: The name Eutychus comes from ancient Greek and literally means "fortunate, happy" (composed of "eu" = well, good, and "tyche" = fortune, chance). It is a common Greek name of the time, expressing the wish that the person be favored by luck.
G2161.emploi: Eutychus appears only once in the Bible, in Acts 20:9, during a memorable episode of Paul's missionary journey. He is known only by this brief mention: an ordinary young man from Troas, asleep during a long sermon, who becomes the subject of a resurrection miracle. His story illustrates the seriousness and length of apostolic teachings, and the power of Jesus' name to bring the dead back to life.
G2161.portee: The story of Eutychus shows us that even in difficult moments and human weaknesses, God is present. It is also a reminder of the power of Paul's apostolic ministry, capable not only of teaching but also of restoring life. Finally, this episode reveals the faith and dedication of early believers, who gathered for long periods to listen to the Word of God.

sens: The favorable opinion one has of someone, their good name
The praise, the commendation given to someone or received
G2162.detail:
1. A good reputation is what is said well of a person, the good name they enjoy among others. It is the opposite of a bad reputation ("disfavor"). In 2 Corinthians 6:8, Paul lists the oppositions faced by the apostles: they are received sometimes with glory, sometimes with disgrace, sometimes with a bad reputation, sometimes with a good reputation.
2. More broadly, it is also the praise, the honorable words addressed to someone or that they enjoy. It is the credit, the honor recognized to them.
G2162.origine: The word comes from "eu" (good) and "pheme" (word, rumor). It literally denotes a word of good omen, a favorable word. It is the opposite of "dysphemia" (bad word, bad reputation). In the Greek Old Testament, the word often translates the Hebrew that means glory or honor.
G2162.emploi: The word appears only once in 2 Corinthians 6:8, in a list of contrasts faced by the servants of Christ. Paul enumerates how the world receives the apostles: sometimes praised, sometimes blamed, sometimes spoken ill of, sometimes spoken well of. This passage shows that true servants of God should expect their reputation to fluctuate according to the world's judgment, which can be as unjust as it can be favorable.
G2162.portee: This word invites us to recognize that a good reputation is not the criterion of truth or integrity. Paul reminds us that the apostles remain true even when they are regarded as impostors, and that one can enjoy a good reputation without being faithful to God. The Christian should seek first the approval of the Lord, not that of the world.

sens: Who deserves approval, esteem
Who has a good reputation
Who inspires words of praise
G2163.detail:
1. The word designates what is worthy of approval and esteem — that which can be praised without fear and with full confidence. In Philippians 4:8, Paul lists the thoughts worthy of occupying the believer's mind: after the just, the pure, and the lovely comes what "deserves" approval, that is, what naturally garners adherence and honor.
2. More broadly, it refers to what has a good reputation, what is spoken well of — that which inspires favorable and propitious words. The underlying image is that of happy omens: a "meritorious" word or action is like a favorable augury that can be stated without risk.
G2163.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: "eu" (well) and "phêmê" (word, reputation, fame). It literally designates one who speaks good words or propitious words. The root "phêmê" is found in other Greek words related to fame and speech. This composition reflects a classical Greek view: to be well spoken of is to have merit and honor.
G2163.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 4:8, where Paul lists eight qualities that should occupy the Christian's thoughts. It is grouped with terms like "true," "honorable," "just," "pure," "lovely" — all positive moral and spiritual qualities. Its context is clearly ethical and pastoral: Paul urges mental restraint, to cultivate lofty thoughts. The word emphasizes that these objects of reflection are not only correct but also deserve general esteem and the adherence of the heart.
G2163.portee: This word reminds the believer that their thoughts must be worthy of honor — not only just but also commendable in the eyes of all. It invites a discipline of the mind: not to let thoughts wander towards what is ambiguous or degrading, but to direct them towards what naturally garners approval. It is an invitation to moral nobility, reflecting the holiness of God.

sens: To produce a large quantity of harvest or fruit
To be fertile and abundant in production
To have great productivity
To experience success and abundance
G2164.detail:
1. The primary meaning is agricultural: a land that produces much yields a great harvest, it is fertile and generous — this is the concrete image Jesus speaks of in Luke 12:16, where the rich man's lands yield much.
2. By extension, it conveys the idea of abundant and fruitful production, whether in crops or results — anything that bears fruit in quantity.
3. Figuratively, it means to have success, to experience prosperity and abundance in one's endeavors.
4. The word can also evoke the idea of produced wealth, of goods accumulated through this fertility — which is the situation of the character in the parable.
G2164.origine: The word is composed of "eu" (well, good, happy) and "phoreo" (to bear, to produce). It literally evokes "to bear well," "to produce well." The root "phoreo" is found in many Greek words related to production and transport. It is a word that emphasizes not only fertility but also the excellence and success of that fertility.
G2164.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 12:16, in the parable that Jesus tells His disciples about the rich man whose lands yield much. Jesus uses this term to show the context of extreme material prosperity of the character — a situation that leads him to pride and forgetfulness of God. The word thus describes agricultural and economic success, which becomes the starting point of Jesus' critique against greed and lack of generosity.
G2164.portee: This parable teaches that material abundance, even when it comes from our honest work, should not become the object of our trust or pride. The rich man in Luke 12 forgets that his life does not belong to him — he accumulates without sharing or serving God. For the Christian, the question is not whether their efforts produce much, but whether they remain attached to God and others in this prosperity. Abundance should inspire generosity, not selfishness.

sens: to make joyful, gladden, to bring joy to someone
to be in joy, to rejoice, to experience gladness
to celebrate, to have fun, to take pleasure in celebrating
to manifest joy through shouts or acclamations
G2165.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to make someone joyful, to give them joy. It is the action of cheering up a person in need: the father of the prodigal son wants to "be glad and rejoice" because his lost son is found (Luke 15:32). This is also what happens when one encounters a sad word: Paul says he does not want to sadden the Corinthians, but rather to rejoice them (2 Corinthians 2:2).
2. The passive or internal sense refers to the state of one who experiences joy, who exults in happiness. "My heart is glad" (Acts 2:26), or when the disciples "began to rejoice" (Luke 15:24) upon seeing their master or celebrating a happy return.
3. The word also applies to festivities, banquets, joyful celebrations. When the rich man "rejoices" every day (Luke 16:19), he indulges in pleasure and feasting. This also occurs when a great feast is held in honor of a happy event (Luke 15:23-24).
4. In a collective or liturgical context, the word expresses proclaimed, shouted, shared joy: "Rejoice with His people!" (Romans 15:10) invites the nations to shout for joy together with the people of God, or the creatures of heaven who rejoice (Revelation 12:12).
G2165.origine: The verb comes from the Greek adjective εὖ ("well") and φρήν ("heart, spirit"), literally "to have a good heart" or "to have a content heart." In the Greek of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), it often translates the Hebrew verb שָׂמַח (samah), which means "to rejoice, to be glad" and which is the classic expression of religious joy in Israel. This image of the happy, content heart is at the core of the word: joy comes from the heart and fills the whole being.
G2165.emploi: The verb appears 14 times in the New Testament, especially in Luke and Revelation. In Luke, it colors scenes of joyful celebration: the banquet of the prodigal son (Luke 15:23-24, 32), the rich man who feasts (Luke 16:19), or the counsel to the soul to rejoice in abundance (Luke 12:19). In Acts, it is Peter's heart filled with joy (Acts 2:26), or the joyful idolatry of the golden calf (Acts 7:41). Paul uses it to invite to rejoice with the people of God (Romans 15:10) and in a prophetic citation (Galatians 4:27). Revelation reserves it for eschatological joys: the inhabitants of heaven rejoice at the fall of Babylon (Revelation 11:10, 12:12, 18:20). The word everywhere expresses a loud, communal joy, manifested — not a silent inner peace.
G2165.portee: This word reminds the believer that the Bible does not despise carnal and festive joy, but roots it in the action of God. The joy of the return of the prodigal son reflects the joy of heaven over a sinner who repents. To rejoice is not frivolity: it is to recognize that God is at work, that life has meaning, that salvation deserves to be celebrated. The invitation to rejoice together, with the people, calls for a joy that does not isolate but unites, creating communion.

sens: great river of the Middle East
river that marks a boundary of the known world of the ancients
G2166.detail:
1. The Euphrates is the great river that flows in Mesopotamia, in the ancient Middle East. It is one of the two major rivers of this region (along with the Tigris). In Revelation, it is referred to as "the great river Euphrates" (Revelation 9:14; 16:12), highlighting its geographical and symbolic importance.
2. In John's vision, the Euphrates also represents a boundary of the known world and a place of power. Its waters are guarded by four angels, and when they dry up, they allow "the kings from the East" to pass (Revelation 16:12). The river acts as a natural barrier which, once crossed, heralds major events.
G2166.origine: The name Euphrates comes from the Greek Euphratēs (Εὐφράτης), which reproduces the Akkadian and Hebrew name of this major river of the Middle East. The word is also known in the Hebrew Old Testament in the form Perat. It is a very ancient geographical name, attested in Mesopotamian texts and used as such in Greek and Hebrew because it designates a specific place well identified by all the peoples of the region.
G2166.emploi: The Euphrates appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Revelation. In Revelation 9:14, John sees four angels bound at the great river Euphrates, and he hears an order to release them. In Revelation 16:12, during the pouring of the sixth bowl, the waters of the Euphrates dry up to prepare the way for the kings of the East. These two occurrences make the Euphrates a key element of the eschatological vision: it embodies both immense military power (the kings of the East) and a boundary of the world that God controls.
G2166.portee: For the Christian reader, the Euphrates in Revelation reminds us that even the major geopolitical powers and natural boundaries of the world are under God's sovereign control. This invites the believer to look beyond present political and geographical realities and to place their trust in the One who governs history according to His plan.

sens: feeling of happiness and inner satisfaction
glee, joyfulness of the heart
satisfaction from enjoying goods or blessings received
G2167.detail:
1. Joy is the deep feeling of happiness and satisfaction that fills the heart. It is a positive emotion, an inner gladness. In Acts 2:28, Peter quotes the Psalm saying to his listeners: "You will make me full of joy in Your presence," expressing how the closeness of God brings inner fulfillment.
2. This word also denotes a joyfulness of heart, a joyful and positive disposition. It is often linked to divine blessing and the awareness of received goods. In Acts 14:17, Paul describes how God fills the hearts of men with joy by granting them abundant food and fruitful seasons: joy arises from recognizing divine goodness.
3. Biblical joy is not a superficial lightness, but a deep satisfaction attached to the experience of God's blessings — His presence, provision, grace. It is the fruit of recognizing and receiving God's gifts.
G2167.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "euphron" (having a good heart, joyful), composed of "eu" (well) and "phren" (the heart, the mind). Its etymology reveals the meaning: a joy that comes from the well-being of the heart and soul. In Hebrew, it often translates the word "simha" (שִׂמְחָה), which also expresses joy and gladness, particularly that which accompanies celebrations and divine blessings.
G2167.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Greek New Testament, both in Acts. In Acts 2:28, in Peter's speech at Pentecost, joy is presented as the direct fruit of God's presence among His people. In Acts 14:17, Paul reminds the inhabitants of Lystra that God fills human hearts with joy through His generosity and blessings. Both passages emphasize that true joy comes from God — either through His immediate presence or through His concrete benefits. It is a joy that transcends mere emotion: it is a response of the heart to divine goodness.
G2167.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that joy is a deep spiritual reality, rooted in the experience of God and His blessings. It is not a fleeting emotion dependent on circumstances, but the fruit of recognizing divine presence and generosity. Joy thus becomes a testimony of God's grace: when the heart is filled with joy in God, it manifests the reality of His presence and love.

sens: Feeling of gratitude, recognition towards someone
Act of expressing gratitude, action of thanking
Formula or prayer to give thanks
In Christian worship, blessing or consecration
G2169.detail:
1. The feeling of gratitude is the deep recognition one feels towards the one who has done good to them: in Acts 24:3, Paul expresses his "thanksgiving" to Felix for the reforms he has brought to the nation.
2. Thanksgiving is the act of thanking, the expression of this recognition: in Philippians 4:6, the believer must make their requests to God "with thanksgiving," that is, while thanking.
3. It is also a specific formula or prayer through which one gives thanks: in 1 Timothy 2:1, we are urged to make "thanksgivings" for all men, a supplication addressed to God.
4. In ecclesial life and worship, it is the blessing or consecration of bread and wine: the word designates the very heart of the Supper, when we give thanks to God for the gift of Christ.
G2169.origine: The word comes from the Greek "eucharistos" (thankful, full of grace), composed of "eu" (well) and "charis" (grace, favor). Its basic image is that of a soul receiving good as a grace and, in return, recognizing the source. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew verb to give thanks, to express recognition before God for His benefits.
G2169.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the New Testament, especially in the Pauline epistles (2 Corinthians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Timothy, 1 Thessalonians) and in Revelation. Paul uses it to urge believers to thank God in all circumstances: in Colossians 4:2, "continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving"; in Philippians 4:6, requests must be accompanied by thanksgiving. In 2 Corinthians 9:12, aid to the poor produces abundant thanksgivings to God. In the cultic context (1 Corinthians 14:16, Revelation 4:9, 7:12), the word designates the blessing and praise addressed to God in the assembly. The meaning thus varies from inner gratitude to its communal and liturgical expression.
G2169.portee: Thanksgiving reveals that the Christian faith is not a mere cold obedience, but a joyful response to God's goodness. Thanking God is to recognize His gifts and grace at every moment, even in trials. For the believer, cultivating thanksgiving transforms the heart, frees it from anxiety, and unites it with the community in praise. It is also to understand that the Supper itself is an act of thanksgiving, a memorial of Christ's supreme gift.

sens: Who feels gratitude, recognition towards one who has done good
Who expresses gratitude through words or actions
Of a gracious and benevolent nature
Worthy of recognition, pleasant
G2170.detail:
1. Thankful describes one who feels gratitude deep in their heart for a benefit received. It is the inner state of one who knows they have been done good and appreciates it. In Colossians 3:15, Paul urges believers to be thankful, which means cultivating this attitude of heart towards what God and others do for us.

2. Gratitude does not remain locked in the heart: it is expressed, manifested through gestures, words, or simply through a visible attitude of gratitude. The word suggests an active attitude that shines through in our relationships.

3. At a broader level, the word can describe a person or action of a gracious and pleasant nature, something that naturally pleases and inspires benevolence around oneself.

4. By extension, one can qualify as thankful that which deserves gratitude, that which is worthy of recognition and naturally inspires the favor of others.
G2170.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: eu (well) and charizesthai (to please, to grant a favor). Its original meaning is that of an action or attitude that pleases, that is agreeable. The element eu- gives the word a positive nuance, while charizesthai evokes the idea of gift and favor. It is the word used to express gratitude towards one who has done good to us, recognizing their benevolent gesture.
G2170.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 3:15, where Paul urges the Colossians to be thankful. In this context, gratitude is part of the exhortation to let the peace of Christ rule in the heart and in the body of the Church. It is a virtue related to Christian communal life and the appreciation of what God has done. Although rare in the New Testament Greek, the word expresses a fundamental attitude of faith: that of perceiving and valuing received gifts.
G2170.portee: To be thankful is to recognize that life and its benefits are not taken for granted, that they are gifts. For the Christian, cultivating this attitude towards God and others transforms the heart and strengthens peace in the community. It is a spiritual posture that frees from bitterness and anchors trust in God, and it fosters harmony in fraternal relationships in Christ.

sens: A solemn commitment to God, a promise made to God to do something or to refrain from something in exchange for His blessing or help.
A request addressed to God, a supplication to obtain His help or grace.
G2171.detail:
1. A vow is a promise made to God in the form of a personal commitment: one promises to do or not do something, with the aim of obtaining His support or blessing. In Acts 18:18, Paul had his head shaved because he had made a vow — probably a promise made to God in connection with a period of consecration. It is a serious religious act, a contract between man and God.
2. Prayer is the cry of the heart to God, the request, the supplication. In James 5:15, "the prayer of faith" refers to this confident intercession by which one implores God for healing: one prays with confidence that God will act. The word can also simply refer to the act of praying, the expression of one's needs to God.
G2171.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to pray, to wish, to desire" (εὔχομαι). It is the act or object of this prayer addressed to God. In the ancient Greek translations of the Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew "vow" (נָדַר), which evokes the idea of a word given to God, a solemn promise. The two meanings (vow and prayer) remain linked: both are forms of communication with God, serious and personal.
G2171.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in important contexts. Two occurrences refer to a vow in the strict sense: Acts 18:18 and 21:23, where Paul and others made vows, probably related to Jewish practices of temporary consecration. One occurrence refers to prayer in James 5:15, where the "prayer of faith" is presented as powerful for the healing of the sick. The word retains this dual meaning: commitment to God on one side, supplicatory prayer on the other, both expressing a serious relationship with God.
G2171.portee: This word reminds the Christian of two essential aspects of their relationship with God: on one hand, the seriousness of committing to God — the promises made to Him are not to be taken lightly — and on the other hand, the power of confident prayer to obtain what one truly desires. The prayer of faith, in particular, shows that God listens and acts on behalf of those who seek Him sincerely.

sens: to address a request to God
to ardently wish for something
to pray for someone
to express a vow or desire
G2172.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to address a request, a supplication to God. It is an attitude of trust where one lays out their needs or desires before the Lord. In James 5:16, the apostle urges to "pray for one another," which shows that one can intercede for someone else before God.

2. The word also carries the idea of ardently wishing, intensely desiring. In Romans 9:3, Paul says he "would" be accursed for his brothers — he expresses a deep wish, a heartfelt desire that stems from his love.

3. To pray can also simply express a formal request, with less solemnity than liturgical prayer. In Acts 27:29, the crew of the ship "waited" for the day — here the word means to hope or wish for the arrival of the day.

4. The word finally denotes the expression of a vow or a collective prayer. In 2 Corinthians 13:9, Paul speaks of what we "ask in our prayers," showing that the word refers to the act of praying itself.
G2172.origine: The verb comes from an ancient Greek root that expresses the idea of saying, formulating, expressing a wish. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this Greek verb mainly translates the word נָדַד (to make a vow) and also עָתַר (to intercede, to implore). This Hebrew root shows that to pray is primarily to pronounce words addressed to God, to formulate a vow or a desire before Him.
G2172.emploi: The verb appears 7 times in the Greek New Testament, concentrated in the Pauline epistles and in the epistle of James. Paul uses it to describe personal prayer (Romans 9:3, where he wishes to be accursed for his brothers), intercession (2 Corinthians 13:7, where he prays for the Corinthians to do good), and specific requests to God (Acts 26:29, where he prays that his listeners become Christians). In James 5:16, the context reminds us that the prayer of the righteous is very effective. The word is also used with a lighter nuance: in Acts 27:29, wishing for the safe arrival of the day. The usage shows that "to pray" goes beyond mere words — it is to engage one's heart in a request to God.
G2172.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that prayer is not a practice reserved for exceptional moments, but the natural expression of the Christian desire to intercede for others and to entrust one's wishes to God. Paul's example in Romans 9:3 shows that authentic prayer costs something — it engages the whole person, even their love for others. Discovering this verb also helps to grasp that to pray is primarily to pronounce, express, formulate: it is to make concrete through words the trust one places in God.

sens: That can serve, that is helpful, that is profitable
That is capable of performing its function or task well
That is able to produce a good result or a beneficial effect
G2173.detail:
1. The word describes something or someone that can serve concretely, that provides a practical service. A vessel can be useful to the master if it fulfills its function well (2 Timothy 2:21); Mark is useful to Paul for ministry, meaning he can truly help him in his apostolic work (2 Timothy 4:11).
