2. Usefulness implies an aptitude: to be useful means to be capable of doing what one exists for or is destined to do. Onesimus becomes useful, whereas before he was useless; the change comes from a transformation that finally makes him capable of serving (Philemon 1:11).
3. The word applies to what produces good, profit. A Christian who purifies himself from bad influences becomes a useful vessel, fit for every good work: his life itself becomes an instrument that God can use.
G2173.origine: The Greek word comes from "eu" (good) and "chraomai" (to use, to employ). Etymologically, it means "well employable." Its opposite in the Bible is "achrontos" (useless), which shows that usefulness is a relative quality: the same object or person can become useful or useless depending on the circumstances and transformations it undergoes.
G2173.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in Paul, and always to speak of a concrete and personal usefulness. In 2 Timothy 2:21, it is a vessel that is useful to the master. In 2 Timothy 4:11, it is a person (Mark) who is useful for a task (the ministry). In Philemon 1:11, the same word returns with force: Onesimus, once useless, has become useful. Paul plays on this contrast to show the radical transformation that faith works in us. Usefulness is always linked to a capacity to serve or to perform a task well.
G2173.portee: This word reminds every Christian that they are called to become "useful" — that is, capable of rendering service, contributing to the good of the Kingdom, serving as an instrument in the hands of the Lord. It also encourages us to see that spiritual transformation is not just an internal matter: it makes us capable of truly serving. For churches, this word raises the question: are we useful for ministry? Have we allowed the Lord to purify us so that He can employ us?

sens: To have courage, to feel morally strengthened
To regain confidence and hope
To be comforted in a difficulty
G2174.detail:
1. To be encouraged means to regain courage and moral strength in the face of a difficult situation. It is to feel revitalized internally. Paul uses this word in Philippians 2:19 to express how he hopes to be comforted by learning news from the church in Philippi through Timothy.
2. The word also evokes the idea of regaining confidence and hope when one needs it. It is the opposite of discouragement: it is to stand up again, to be filled anew with assurance to continue.
3. To be encouraged is to receive moral support that allows us to persevere. In the Pauline context, it is particularly the assurance that the churches are doing well that strengthens the apostle.
G2174.origine: The Greek word comes from two parts: "eu" (good) and "psyche" (soul, heart). Literally, it means "to have a good heart" or "to have a good disposition of soul." It is a compound that expresses a positive inner state — one who has courage and moral vigor. This image of the soul or heart being strengthened is common in the Greek language to describe a person's emotional and moral state.
G2174.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 2:19. Paul writes to the church in Philippi that he hopes to send Timothy soon, and that he himself will be "encouraged" by learning how the Philippians are doing. In this context, the apostle expresses his need to receive reassuring news about the life of the church to be comforted in his ministry and concerns. It is a verb that captures the relational and pastoral aspect of encouragement: Paul finds courage in the communion and well-being of his churches.
G2174.portee: This word reminds us that mutual encouragement is at the heart of church life. Paul, despite his apostolic authority, needs to be comforted by his brothers. This shows us that receiving news from other believers, knowing that the churches are doing well, that faith is growing, is a deep source of spiritual strength. For the Christian, it is a call to regularly share what revives faith — testimonies, answered prayers, God's faithfulness.

sens: Fragrance, pleasant aroma
Image of an offering, a sacrifice that pleases God
Expression of divine acceptance, of God's favor
G2175.detail:
1. In the literal sense, a pleasant smell, a fragrance. It is the concrete image of an aroma that pleases the senses. In 2 Corinthians 2:15, Paul uses it to describe the fragrance of Christ that emanates from His messengers before God.

2. An offering, a sacrifice that rises to God and pleases Him. In the Old Testament, when an animal was burned on the altar, its smoke and smell ascended to God: it was a sign that the sacrifice was accepted. In Ephesians 5:2, Christ offered Himself "as a fragrant offering and sacrifice" — His sacrifice is what perfectly pleases God the Father.

3. The sign that God accepts a person, a gift, or a life. In Philippians 4:18, Paul calls the gift from the Philippians "a fragrant offering": it is not just a useful gift, but an act that rises to God and receives His blessing.
G2175.origine: The word comes from the Greek "eu" (good) and "ozo" (to smell, to exhale an odor). The Greek Old Testament rendered it with the Hebrew word "nihoach" (pleasant), which evokes the soothing smell of an accepted sacrifice. This image of the "good smell rising to God" often appears in the Torah and in Ezekiel: it symbolizes divine acceptance.
G2175.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in Paul's writings, always in the context of sacrifice or divine favor. In 2 Corinthians 2:15, Paul describes the apostles as a "fragrance of Christ" before God — their testimony is a living offering. In Ephesians 5:2, Christ's sacrifice is itself described as a "fragrant offering", the perfect gift to the Father. In Philippians 4:18, Paul transforms the material gift from the Philippians into a spiritual sacrifice, a "fragrant offering" pleasing to God. Each time, the word evokes divine acceptance and conformity to the gift that it expects.
G2175.portee: This image teaches the reader that their gifts, love, and life offered to God are not invisible: they "rise" to God like a pleasant smell, and God accepts them. It also reminds that Christ's sacrifice is not a trivial act, but the offering that perfectly pleases God. It invites the Christian to offer their life as a "fragrant offering" — not out of vanity, but because this image shows that God sees and blesses every sincere gift.

sens: Located on the left side of the body or of an oriented space
Situated to the south (in the Hebrew geographical perspective)
Of bad omen, of sinister presage (ancient euphemistic sense)
G2176.detail:
1. The primary and concrete sense: what is located to the left, in relation to the right side of the body or a spatial orientation. It is the side opposite to the right. The Gospels use it mainly to describe positions in the kingdom and at the cross: the two criminals are crucified "one on His right, and the other on His left" (Matthew 27:38), and at the final judgment, the goats are placed "on His left" while the sheep are on the right (Matthew 25:33, 41).
2. In ancient Hebrew geography, "left" also designates the south, as one is facing east. This sense persists in biblical Greek, notably in Acts 21:3 and Revelation 10:2.
3. An ancient figurative sense, euphemistic: the word literally meant "of good omen" (from "eu", good, and "onoma", name), but it was used by superstition to designate what was actually sinister or of bad omen — the left being considered unfortunate in many ancient cultures.
G2176.origine: The Greek word composed of "eu" (good) and "onoma" (name) literally means "of good name". It is only a euphemism: a positive expression is used to designate what was feared, the left. In Hebrew, the underlying word is "semol" (שְׂמֹאול), which simply means "left". Biblical Greek preferred this term over the direct word "aristeros" (ἀριστερός), likely out of respect for the ancient superstition that viewed the left as inauspicious.
G2176.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Matthew and Mark, as well as in Acts and Revelation. Matthew uses it mainly in the context of the final judgment and the Passion: the goats on the left receive the curse (25:41), while at the cross, a criminal crucified on the left of Christ evokes this separation of destinies. Mark uses "left" when James and John request places of honor on the right and left in the kingdom (10:40, 15:27). The word retains its objective spatial value but takes on a theological resonance: the left becomes the sign of rejection, while the right symbolizes favor and honor.
G2176.portee: Spiritually, the right-left distinction in these passages symbolizes divine judgment: the right is the place of honor and salvation, the left that of rejection. By reading that the cursed are on the left of the Lord (Matthew 25:41), the believer understands that our choices have eternal consequences visible at judgment. This calls for vigilance and obedience.

sens: To leap onto someone with violence and impetuosity
To attack someone in a brutal and sudden manner
G2177.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of jumping or leaping onto someone with force and aggressiveness. It is a violent and impulsive movement, like that of a beast leaping to attack. In Acts 19:16, the man possessed by an evil spirit "jumps on" the seven sons of Sceva with such fury that he injures them and puts them to flight: it is a sudden and fierce aggression.
2. In a figurative sense, the word can describe a moral or spiritual attack — a brutal assault against someone. The context of Acts 19 shows a demonic possession that manifests through this extreme physical violence: the evil spirit takes possession of the man's body and drives him to strike violently.
G2177.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "epi" (upon) and the verb "hallomai" (to jump, to leap). It evokes the image of a jump or a brutal rush. The Greek root "hallomai" also appears in other words describing lively and sudden movements. This verb appears in the Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament) to translate the Hebrew "tsalakh", which can mean to succeed or prosper in certain contexts, but here it carries the idea of leaping onto something with force.
G2177.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: Acts 19:16. In this key passage, during Paul's ministry in Ephesus, seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva attempt to exorcise a man by invoking the name of Jesus without true faith. The evil spirit in this man recognizes them and reacts with extreme violence: he "jumps on" all seven at once, strikes them, and injures them so severely that they flee naked and wounded. The verb emphasizes the sudden ferocity and demonic power expressed through the body of the possessed man.
G2177.portee: This passage reveals that evil spirits do not fear empty religious formulas: what matters is true faith in Jesus and His real authority. The account also shows that demonic attacks can be violent and terrifying — but the context (a few verses later) reveals that the name of Jesus, invoked in faith, triumphs completely. For the believer, this is a call not to play with spiritual realities, but to rely on the authentic power of Christ.

sens: one single time, in a definitive and irreversible manner
at one single moment, simultaneously
G2178.detail:
1. The primary meaning expresses the idea of an act that does not repeat, that occurs only once and produces a permanent and complete effect. It is the image of a decisive event that concludes a series: Jesus "died once for all" (Romans 6:10), he will never have to die again. The same applies to his sacrifice: he "did it once for all by offering himself" (Hebrews 7:27), unlike the repeated sacrifices of the old covenant.
2. A second, rarer usage simply denotes simultaneity or accumulation at one single moment: Jesus "appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once" (1 Corinthians 15:6) means that he showed himself to all these brothers together, at the same instant.
G2178.origine: The Greek word is composed of "ἐπί" (upon, at) and "ἅπαξ" (once). The adverb "ἅπαξ" expresses uniqueness, and the prefix reinforces the idea of an action accomplished in its fullness, one time being sufficient. This term appears only in the Greek New Testament and becomes central in Christian theology to express the unique and irrevocable nature of Christ's work.
G2178.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in connection with the sacrificial and redemptive work of Jesus Christ. It is found 4 times in direct relation to the sacrifice: Christ dies once for all (Romans 6:10), offers a unique sacrifice (Hebrews 7:27; 9:12; 10:10). This repetition of the same word in Hebrews emphasizes that the author sees in Jesus the perfect and definitive fulfillment of the sacrificial system of the Old Testament. One usage stands out from this context: 1 Corinthians 15:6, where it describes the appearance of the Resurrected to more than five hundred brothers together.
G2178.portee: This word illuminates the Christian faith regarding the unique and sufficient nature of Christ's work. It affirms that his death and sacrifice do not need to be repeated or supplemented: one offering, one time, has conquered sin and opened eternal access to God. This truth frees the believer from any fear that salvation is incomplete or fragile.

sens: Inhabitant or native of Ephesus, the great city of Asia Minor.
Belonging to the city of Ephesus or its inhabitants.
Faithful Christian of the Church of Ephesus.
G2180.detail:
1. Ephesian primarily refers to an inhabitant or native of Ephesus, a major port city in Asia Minor (present-day Turkey). At the time of the Acts narrative, Ephesus was famous for its temple dedicated to the goddess Diana (Artemis), and it is as proud citizens of this city that the Ephesians shout, "Great is Diana of the Ephesians!" (Acts 19:28, 34).
2. By extension, the word qualifies what belongs to Ephesus or its population: the city clerk addresses the inhabitants by saying, "Men of Ephesus" (Acts 19:35), as all citizens were concerned with the honor and prosperity of their city.
3. In the New Testament epistles (Ephesians, 2 Timothy), the word applies to Christians converted in Ephesus who formed the local Church of that city, distinct from other Christian communities.
G2180.origine: The word comes from the geographical root Ephesus, the name of the city in ancient Greek. Ephesus was one of the major cities of the Mediterranean basin, founded as an Ionian Greek colony and becoming the capital of the Roman province of Asia. The term "Ephesian" simply adds to the name of the city to form a relational adjective.
G2180.emploi: The word "Ephesian" appears 6 times in the New Testament. Three times in a dramatic context: during the riot provoked by the silversmith Demetrius concerning the Diana of the Ephesians (Acts 19:28, 34, 35). Once it qualifies Trophimus, a companion of Paul, as Ephesian by origin (Acts 21:29). Finally, it appears twice in the greetings of the epistles addressed to the Church of Ephesus (Ephesians 6:24 and 2 Timothy 4:22), where it may refer to the believers of this Church. The context varies: from urban civic duty to Christian religious sentiment.
G2180.portee: This word reminds us that the Gospel is rooted in real cities and concrete peoples. Ephesus was a major center of ancient paganism, and it is there that Paul established one of the most important Churches of his time. For the contemporary Christian reader, this shows how God transforms great cities and their inhabitants, and how the early Church grew in metropolises hostile to the Christian message.

sens: Major port city of Asia Minor (present-day Turkey)
Center of the worship of the goddess Artemis
Place of apostolic meetings and controversies
Christian community established by Paul
Church recipient of an apostolic letter
G2181.detail:
1. Ephesus is a large coastal city in Asia Minor (region of present-day Turkey), an important commercial and religious crossroads. Paul arrives there during his missionary journeys and leaves his companions (Acts 18:19); the name of the Lord is glorified through the account of miracles (Acts 19:17).
2. The city was especially known for its monumental temple dedicated to the goddess Artemis, whose worship generated a prosperous trade in small shrines. Paul had to face opposition from the craftsmen who lived off this trade (Acts 19:26).
3. It is a place of significant meetings: Apollos, a man well-versed in the Scriptures, comes there (Acts 18:24), and Paul teaches in the synagogue and later in the hall of Tyrannus.
4. Paul establishes an important Christian community in Ephesus, staying there for a long time and entrusting Timothy with a pastoral charge (1 Timothy 1:3).
5. The epistle addressed to the Ephesians (Ephesians 1:1) and the mentions in Revelation (Revelation 1:11; 2:1) show that this church was one of the most prestigious in the Mediterranean world.
G2181.origine: The Greek name Ephesus (Ἔφεσος) refers to the historical city founded by the Ionians, one of the twelve major Greek cities of Asia Minor. Its name may derive from its geographical position, but the exact etymology remains debated among historians. The city appears in ancient records as early as the 11th century BC and gradually became a leading commercial and religious metropolis.
G2181.emploi: Ephesus appears 16 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the narrative of Acts and in the Pauline letters. In Acts, it is the scene of Paul’s apostolic mission: his arrivals (18:19, 19:1), his teachings, and the miracles that occur there (19:17). Paul stays there longer than anywhere else, attracting the hostility of the merchants of temple statuettes (19:26). It also appears in his correspondence: Paul entrusts Timothy with a pastoral mission in Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:3; 2 Timothy 1:18; 4:12), and the letter to the Ephesians is addressed to this community (Ephesians 1:1). In Revelation, the church of Ephesus is the first of the seven churches of Asia addressed (Revelation 1:11; 2:1).
G2181.portee: Ephesus embodies the success of Paul’s mission in Asia Minor and the emergence of a flourishing church in pagan land. It shows how the Gospel penetrates urban centers, provokes social transformations (the decline of religious commerce), and establishes communities mature enough to receive apostolic letters. For the contemporary Christian, Ephesus reminds us that the Christian faith is rooted in concrete history, in real cities and people, and that it transforms societies from within.

sens: one who invents, discovers ways to do evil
one who invents or creates something new, especially malicious methods
one who is clever or cunning in committing evil
G2182.detail: 1. The word designates someone who "finds" or "invents" — that is, who imagines and develops — ways to do evil or harm others. It is not simply about doing harm, but doing so creatively, finding new methods. Paul uses it in Romans 1:30 to describe those who, in their rebellion against God, become ingenious and inventive in evil: they do not merely commit wicked acts, but they find new, even worse ones. It conveys the idea of someone who "forges" or "manufactures" evil with a kind of perverse talent.
G2182.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to discover, find, invent." The root evokes the idea of searching for and finding something new or hidden. The prefix "epi" (ἐπί) intensifies the action. In Hebrew, a similar expression is found in 2 Maccabees 7:31, where it describes an "inventor of wickedness." It is a rather rare word in biblical Greek, emphasizing the active and creative aspect of evil.
G2182.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 1:30, where Paul lists the vices of those who, having rejected the knowledge of God, have given themselves over to ungodliness and depravity. In this list of serious sins — gossips, slanderers, arrogant, haughty — the term "inventor of evil" emphasizes that ungodliness is not limited to isolated wicked acts, but becomes an organized and ingenious enterprise. It is the portrait of humanity in rupture with God, who even perverts its intelligence and creativity in the service of evil.
G2182.portee: This word invites the believer to ask whether, by rejecting God, they risk putting their intelligence to the service of evil rather than good. It shows that sin is never trivial: it can become a kind of system, where one "invents" new ways to distance oneself from God and do harm. For the Christian, it is a call to place their ingenuity and creativity in the service of God and the good of others.

sens: Division of service in the temple
Group of priests assigned in rotation to divine service
Period of service assigned to a particular group
G2183.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a division of cultic work: the orderly succession of daily services that were to take place in the temple, day after day. It is the image of a task that is regularly repeated, in rotation.
2. More specifically, it refers to a group or class of priests who were entrusted, in turn, with service in the Jerusalem temple. In Luke 1:5, Zechariah belongs "to the class of Abijah," which means he was part of a specific team of priests.
3. By extension, it is the period itself during which a class assumed its responsibilities: in Luke 1:8, Zechariah "was performing his duties before God, according to the order of his class," that is, during the week (or time) assigned to his division.
G2183.origine: The word comes from the adjective "ephemeral" ("lasting one day"), composed of "epi" (upon, during) and "day." It thus evokes first what is daily, recurring each day. Applied to temple service, it designates a succession of recurring tasks, entrusted to groups that regularly rotated. Jewish tradition, already visible in 1 Chronicles, had divided the priests into twenty-four classes, each serving in turn at the temple.
G2183.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke 1 (verses 5 and 8), during the account of the angel Gabriel announcing to Zechariah the birth of John the Baptist. These two uses describe exactly the same reality: Zechariah belongs to the class (or division) of Abijah, and it is during his class's turn of service that he performed his priestly duties in the temple. The context shows that this system was well established and regular: each class had its defined responsibilities and scheduled times of service.
G2183.portee: This historical and liturgical detail reminds us that the life of the Israelite temple was organized with precision and regularity, and that Zechariah was a man integrated into this sacred system established long ago. It is in the faithful fulfillment of these ordinary tasks that the extraordinary divine intervention occurs: God meets Zechariah in the midst of his daily service, showing us that the Lord often reveals Himself amid our regular and dedicated occupations.

sens: Lasting one day
Needed every day
Ordinary, mundane
G2184.detail:
1. The word literally evokes what lives only for a day — like an ephemeral flower that blooms in the morning and withers in the evening. It is what is limited to a single day, of very brief duration.

2. Applied to what repeats or is needed daily: the daily bread (James 2:15) refers to the bread and provisions that a man needs to survive day after day. It is the immediate necessity, that which must be renewed constantly.

3. By extension, the word can qualify what is ordinary, simple, without brilliance — because it recurs every day and is nothing extraordinary.
G2184.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: "epi" (upon, for) and "hēméra" (the day). Literally "for a day." The basic image is that of what exists or lasts only for the current day. The same root "hēméra" is found in words that speak of the day or the daily.
G2184.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 2:15, in a call for concrete help towards the poor. The apostle James describes a brother or sister who lacks clothing and the daily food — that is, the vital minimum, the daily necessity for living. The use emphasizes that even the simplest and most ordinary help, the daily bread, must be given out of love.
G2184.portee: This word brings us back to humility and reality. The Bible does not call us to spectacular gestures, but to provide for the simple and daily needs of those who suffer. It is also a call to personal humility: to recognize that we too, like all men, depend on God for our daily bread.

sens: To move to a place, to reach it
To reach someone or something, to join
To arrive at extending one's action or influence to a given limit
G2185.detail:
1. The basic meaning is that of spatial movement: going from one place to another, actually arriving there. It is the simple idea of covering a distance and crossing it (2 Corinthians 10:14: "we have come with the Gospel").

2. By extension, the verb denotes the act of reaching a person or thing, joining or touching it. It is to come up to someone to meet or reach them.

3. In a more figurative sense, it means to extend one's action, influence, or responsibility to a certain limit or boundary. In 2 Corinthians 10:13, Paul uses it to say that the measure God has given him extends precisely to the Corinthians: his area of apostleship "comes up to" this community.
G2185.origine: The Greek verb combines the preposition "epi" (upon, up to) and the root "hikneomai" (to arrive, to reach). This root originally evokes the movement of something that extends or progresses to a given point. The word translates ancient Greek concepts of arrival and extension from Hebrew-Aramaic.
G2185.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians 10, verses 13 and 14, in the context where Paul defends his apostleship to the Corinthians. He uses the word to express that the authority and missionary territory that God has assigned to him extends precisely to Corinth. The verb thus carries both a geographical nuance (the message has reached there) and a missionary one (his field of apostolic action reaches this community). It is a rare word, used to emphasize a limit or boundary reached.
G2185.portee: For the Christian reader, this verb invites reflection on the limits and fields of action that God assigns to each person. Paul acknowledges that his ministry is not meant to extend everywhere, but to a measure determined by God himself. This teaches humility: each servant of God has a domain that is their own, and faithfulness consists in fully exercising it within the boundaries set by the Lord, without claiming an universality that does not belong to them.

sens: To suddenly appear before someone
To present oneself or arrive on the scene
To be present at a given moment
To come unexpectedly, without prior announcement
G2186.detail:
1. To suddenly appear before someone: the word paints the image of an arrival that surprises. In Luke 2:9, the angel of the Lord "appears" to the shepherds, suddenly appearing before them in the brilliance of divine glory. It is a presence that imposes itself unexpectedly.
2. To present oneself or arrive on the scene: it is to show oneself in a specific place to act. When the priests and Sadducees "came upon" Peter and John (Acts 4:1), they came on site to intervene. Similarly, the three men sent from Caesarea "presented themselves" at the door of the house (Acts 11:11).
3. To be present at a given moment: simply to be there at the time of events. Paul says: "I was myself present" when the blood of Stephen was shed (Acts 22:20). He was on the scene, a witness to what was happening.
4. To come unexpectedly, to fall upon someone: the image is that of an impromptu arrival, often carrying significance. The rain "fell" suddenly on the island of Malta (Acts 28:2); trials "will occur" to the inattentive (1 Thessalonians 5:3).
G2186.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "epi" (upon, against) and the verb "histêmi" (to place, to set, to stand). The primitive image is thus "to place upon" or "to stand beside." In the Hebrew and Aramaic of the Old Testament, it often translates roots like "natzab" (to stand, to stand before) or "shith" (to place, to fix). This verb carries the idea of an active and deliberate presence, not passive.
G2186.emploi: The verb appears 21 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles. It describes very varied situations: the coming of angels (Luke 2:9, 24:4), the unexpected arrival of religious authorities (Luke 20:1, Acts 4:1), the presence of someone with a sick person (Luke 4:39, 10:40), the manifestation of natural phenomena like rain (Acts 28:2), or the imminence of future events (1 Thessalonians 5:3, 2 Timothy 4:6). The context determines the nuance: sometimes it is a planned and intentional arrival, sometimes it is a sudden irruption.
G2186.portee: This word reminds the reader that God and his messengers intervene in real time in human history. It also emphasizes the necessity of spiritual vigilance: if angels, apostles, or trials can occur unexpectedly, the Christian must remain alert and ready. It is a word that brings to life the supernatural reality of the New Testament.

sens: Small town in Judea, near Jerusalem
G2187.detail: Ephraim is a small town located in the vicinity of Jerusalem, in the mountains. It is where Jesus withdrew after raising Lazarus, to escape the Jewish authorities who were seeking to kill him (John 11:54). The name does not refer here to the large tribe of Israel of the same name, but to this small village where Jesus stayed discreetly with his disciples before his passion.
G2187.origine: This place bears the name of the historical tribe of Ephraim, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. The name comes from the Hebrew "Ephrayim," which means "double fruitfulness" (from the word "pri": fruit). The tribe of Ephraim occupied the heart of the northern territory of Israel; the small town in Judea mentioned in John 11 may be a locality later renamed after this famous tribe.
G2187.emploi: Ephraim appears only once in the New Testament, in John 11:54. It is a geographical indication: Jesus withdraws to this town after the resurrection of Lazarus, when the Jewish leaders conspire to kill him. This detail emphasizes that Jesus, instead of openly continuing his ministry, chooses a secluded place to protect himself and prepare his disciples for the events to come.
G2187.portee: This passage shows that Jesus, although the powerful Messiah, accepted to temporarily withdraw from danger to preserve his life until the hour set by the Father. For the reader, it is a reminder that God arranges everything according to his plan, including seemingly constraining circumstances.

sens: Direct command addressed to a part of the body to function normally
G2188.detail: 1. This Aramaic word, in the passive form, is an imperative that commands opening. Jesus addresses it to a deaf-mute man (Mark 7:34): the ears must open to hear, and the tongue must be loosed to speak. It is an authoritative command directed at this sick body for healing to take place.
G2188.origine: It is an Aramaic word, the language Jesus spoke daily. It comes from a root meaning to disengage, to free, to open — the idea is that of a barrier falling, of a passage being made. Mark retained the exact word in Aramaic rather than translating it, which shows the importance of this moment: it is the very word of Jesus, direct and powerful.
G2188.emploi: This word appears only once in the entire Bible, in Mark 7:34. Jesus heals a man afflicted with deafness and mutism. After taking him away from the crowd and putting him aside, he sighs (a sign of compassion and seriousness), looks up to heaven, and then pronounces this simple Aramaic command. The effect is immediate: the ears open and the tongue is loosed. This unique cry reinforces its memorable character: it is a word of absolute power.
G2188.portee: This word shows us how Jesus heals. He does not pronounce a magic formula, but acts with compassion and with a natural authority that commands the sick nature to restore itself. For the reader, it is an assurance: Jesus has the power to lift every barrier, every infirmity. It is also an encouragement: his simple and direct words accomplish what our weakness cannot achieve.

sens: state of hostility and opposition between two people or two groups
deep feeling of aversion and hatred
breakdown of peace and communion
G2189.detail:
1. Enmity is primarily the concrete state where two people or two groups find themselves in open opposition: Pilate and Herod "who had been enemies before" (Luke 23:12) — they could not stand each other, refused to see each other. It is the broken relationship, the complete absence of peace.

2. The word also designates the inner feeling that drives this opposition: an aversion, an active hatred. When Paul writes that "the mind of the flesh is enmity against God" (Romans 8:7), he shows that our natural tendency to sin puts us in direct conflict with God — it is a state of hostility of the heart and will.

3. Enmity can be one of the manifestations of sin among others: Paul cites it with "strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger" (Galatians 5:20), as one of the works of the flesh that divide Christians.

4. It is also what separates humanity from God Himself. Jesus destroyed "enmity" on His cross (Ephesians 2:16), that is, the hostility that had arisen between God and sinners. The love of the world is "enmity" against God (James 4:4): one cannot serve two masters, love the world and love God at the same time.
G2189.origine: The Greek word comes from the root of "enemy" (echthros). It designates the state or condition of hostility that exists between enemies — not the enemy itself, but the relationship of enmity. In Hebrew, the Old Testament used words like "aybah" (אֵיבָה) or "sin'ah" (שִׂנְאָה) to express this same idea of enmity, hatred, rupture.
G2189.emploi: The word "enmity" appears 5 times in the New Testament. It first appears to describe a human situation: Pilate and Herod were enemies before finding a common interest against Jesus (Luke 23:12). But especially, Paul uses it to describe a spiritual reality: the enmity between the sinful nature and God (Romans 8:7), among the sins committed by the flesh (Galatians 5:20), between the world and God (James 4:4). The strongest sense is in Ephesians 2:16, where Jesus destroys enmity itself — He reconciles enemies through His cross. The word always marks a deep, personal rupture, whether between humans or between man and God.
G2189.portee: Understanding "enmity" helps the Christian see that sin is not just a list of bad acts: it is an active hostility, a rupture of communion with God. But the heart of the biblical message is that Jesus has "destroyed" this enmity through His death. The cross not only forgave our sins — it changed our relationship with God, moving from hostility to peace. Recognizing where enmity hides in our hearts — in our love for the world, our quarrels, our grudges — allows us to choose the reconciliation that Jesus offers.

sens: One who hates, who harbors hostility
One who opposes, who fights
One who threatens or does harm
The devil, the spiritual adversary
Hostile, filled with hatred (as an adjective)
G2190.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one who actively hates, who feels hostility. It is someone who opposes you by feeling or by action: "If your enemy is hungry, feed him" (Romans 12:20) shows that the enemy is a real person, a living adversary.
2. More broadly, it is one who fights or openly opposes. In Matthew 13:39, Jesus calls the devil "the enemy" who sowed the tares — the one who acts against God's plan.
3. The word also describes the position of one who threatens or does harm: "Until I make your enemies your footstool" (Luke 20:43) speaks of those who oppose Christ and will be defeated.
4. In the spiritual context, it designates Satan himself or the hostile powers against the kingdom of God.
5. Used as an adjective, it expresses hostility, malice: "Enemies in your minds and by your wicked works" (Colossians 1:21) describes an attitude contrary to God.
G2190.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and expresses the idea of hatred. It opposes "beloved" (agapetos). In Hebrew, it primarily translates "aiba" (hostility), which shows that the enemy is not just a physical adversary, but someone with whom there is a rupture, a deep opposition.
G2190.emploi: The word appears 32 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the epistles of Paul. It designates various adversaries: the enemies of the people of God (Luke 1:71, 74), the adversaries of Christ (Luke 20:43), the devil (Matthew 13:39), and the personal enemies of believers (Luke 6:27). Paul also uses it figuratively to describe the condition of a sinner: "Enemies of God" (Romans 5:10, 11:28). The context oscillates between the concrete enemy, political or personal, and the spiritual enemy, Satan or sin.
G2190.portee: This word reminds the Christian that there are real forces opposing God and His people, but also that he must transform his relationship with human enemies: Jesus commands to love one's enemies (Matthew 5:44, Luke 6:27), revealing that even hostility must be overcome by love. This frees from the cycle of vengeance and reveals Christ's ultimate victory over all adversaries.

sens: Venomous snake with a triangular head, dangerous and malevolent
Image of a wicked person, of a corrupt and evil heart
G2191.detail:
1. The viper is a real venomous snake, a living and recognizable animal. In Acts 28:3, a real viper comes out of a pile of brush heated by the fire and attaches itself to Paul's hand.
2. The word also designates the very essence of moral malice. Jesus calls the Pharisees and Sadducees who come for baptism "brood of vipers" (Matthew 3:7 and Luke 3:7), reproaching these religious leaders for their hypocrisy. In Matthew 12:34, He emphasizes that "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks": the word reveals the hidden viper within. The venomous animal becomes the image of a deeply corrupted nature, of a malice that poisons everything it touches.
G2191.origine: The Greek word ἔχιδνα comes from a root that evokes the idea of sinuosity and self-coiling. The viper, by its winding, secretive, and dangerous nature, naturally becomes the biblical symbol of moral evil and deceit. The ancient Hebrew word צפע (tsefa) or similar also designates venomous snakes in the Old Testament.
G2191.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament. Four uses are metaphorical and concentrated in the words of Jesus addressed to the scribes and Pharisees. Jesus does not describe their behavior as bad: He goes deeper, denouncing their very nature, their heart (Matthew 12:34, Matthew 23:33). One use is literal: in Acts 28:3, Paul is bitten by a real viper, an incident that manifests divine protection over the apostle.
G2191.portee: This image teaches that moral corruption comes from the heart and is revealed in words. It warns against religious hypocrisy, which may seem respectable on the outside but hides a wicked nature. For the believer, it is a call to examine one's own heart and not to settle for an outward righteousness.

sens: To hold in one's hand or on oneself
To be in possession of, to own
To carry on or in oneself (clothes, weapons, child)
To keep, preserve, maintain
To maintain a relationship, a quarrel with someone
To be in a state, a condition
G2192.detail:
1. To hold or grasp in one's hand: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear" (Matthew 11:15) — the word describes the simple action of holding something in the hand or keeping it close.
2. To possess, to own: "Jesus said to him, 'If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you possess'" (Matthew 19:21) — here it refers to goods, wealth that one holds and can relinquish.
3. To wear clothing or carry a weapon, or to be pregnant: "John wore a garment of camel's hair" (Matthew 3:4); "a woman in the stony places, where she had not much earth" (Matthew 13:5) — it is to don something or carry it physically.
4. To keep, preserve something in the mind or heart: "holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience" (1 Timothy 3:9) — one retains, preserves something as a precious possession.
5. To have a quarrel or grievance against someone: "if you have something against someone, forgive" (Mark 11:25) — to maintain a conflict, a difficult relationship.
6. To be in a certain physical or moral state: "the sick... those who were possessed by demons" (Matthew 4:24) — describing the situation or condition in which one finds oneself.
G2192.origine: The verb ἔχω comes from a very ancient root meaning "to hold, to grasp." It translates into Greek several Hebrew words (such as "to have," "to possess," "to hold"). It is one of the most frequent verbs in the New Testament: it expresses the fundamental idea of possession, holding, or connection. The word also appears in many compounds (to carry with oneself, to have with oneself, to hold together, etc.).
G2192.emploi: The verb "to have" is one of the most common in the New Testament (632 occurrences). It is used first in a concrete sense: to hold something in the hand (Revelation 5:8), to wear clothing (Matthew 3:4), to be pregnant (Matthew 1:18). It also means "to possess" material goods: "the rich had a great harvest" (Luke 12:16). It extends to the moral and spiritual realm: "to have faith," "to have love," "to have a purpose." It can also indicate necessity or obligation: "I must be baptized by you" (Matthew 3:14). Finally, it simply describes a state: "how are you?" (Acts 15:36).
G2192.portee: This verb reminds us that our possessions, our gifts, and even our lives truly belong to us only in trust. The question of "possessing" often arises in Jesus' teaching: am I a slave to my possessions, or can I let them go? "To have" can also describe our relationships: to have hatred, to have forgiveness. It is a word that invites us to reflect on what we keep deep in our hearts and to whom what we believe we possess truly belongs.

sens: Marking the final point in time: until when something lasts or occurs
Marking the spatial limit: how far an action extends
Indicating duration: as long as, during the time that
Expressing a quantity or a limit measure
Introducing a condition or an event that ends an action
G2193.detail:
1. This is the most common meaning: the word indicates until what precise moment an action continues or stops. For example, in Matthew 1:17, generations are counted "until David," then "until the deportation," then "until Christ" — each point marks where the series ends. In Matthew 26:29, Jesus says he will not drink of the fruit of the vine "until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of my Father": this means that his abstention will last until that precise moment, and not beyond.

2. The word can also mark a limit of space or extension: how far an action extends. In Matthew 27:51, the veil of the temple is torn "from the top to the bottom," showing that the tear extends from one point to another. In Acts 8:40, the deacon Philip runs "until Joppa" — the word marks the end of his journey.

3. Sometimes, especially in Greek poetry, the word means "as long as" or "while," expressing a continuous duration. In John 9:4, Jesus says: "I must work the works of him who sent me, while it is day" — the word indicates the duration of the day as the framework for his action.

4. When speaking of quantities or measures, the word can mark a numerical limit. In Matthew 18:21-22, Peter asks: "Lord, how often shall I forgive my brother? Until seven times?" Jesus replies, "Until seventy times seven," meaning without limit — the number marks the point where the series was supposed to stop, which Jesus exceeds.

5. The word can also introduce a condition or an event that interrupts a previous action. In Matthew 18:30, the unforgiving debtor throws his companion into prison "until he should pay" — the prison will last as long as the debt is not repaid.
G2193.origine: The Greek word ἕως comes from a root that expresses the idea of limit or term. It is related to words that mean "boundary" or "limit" in Indo-European languages. The word has enriched itself in classical Greek to serve as both a conjunction and a preposition or adverb. It often corresponds in the Greek Old Testament to the translation of the Hebrew word עַד (ad), which carries the same sense of limitation or terminus point. It is a very ancient word, attested as early as Homer, which shows how the Greeks thought about temporal and spatial limits.
G2193.emploi: The word ἕως is extremely frequent in the New Testament: it appears about 139 times, present in all the Gospels (especially Matthew and Luke), in Acts, and in the epistles. It primarily serves to mark temporal boundaries: "until David," "until the end of the world," "until now." But it is also used for spatial limits: "until heaven," "until the inside," "until down." In the Gospels, Jesus frequently uses it to speak of his temporal mission ("while it is day") or to state conditions ("until you have paid"). In Paul, the word appears when it comes to deadlines or eschatological ends ("until the mystery of iniquity acts"). The meaning varies according to the context: with the indicative, it marks a real and completed limit; with the subjunctive, it expresses an expectation or a future condition.
G2193.portee: For the Christian, this small word reminds us that time has boundaries: there is a "until" that defines each season of life. By reading that generations stretch "until" Jesus, we understand that human history converges toward him. When Jesus speaks of forgiving "until seventy times seven," he exceeds human limits — the word shows that we tend to count, to measure, and that it calls us to surpass this logic. Finally, this word emphasizes that nothing in this world is without end: sufferings, delays, trials all have a term — a discreet yet profound consolation.

sens: Son of Jacob and Leah
Tribe of Israel descended from Zebulun
Territory occupied by this tribe in Canaan
G2194.detail: 1. Zebulun is the tenth son of Jacob, born of Leah. His Hebrew name means "dwelling" or "habitation." 2. The tribe of Zebulun is one of the twelve tribes of Israel, formed by the descendants of this son of Jacob. At the end of times, Revelation lists the sealed tribes and mentions twelve thousand members of the tribe of Zebulun (Revelation 7:8). 3. The territory of Zebulun was located in Galilee, in northern Israel, near the sea. Capernaum, where Jesus established His ministry, was in this region (Matthew 4:13). Matthew cites a prophecy that designates "the people of Zebulun and Naphtali" as those who would see the light of the Messiah (Matthew 4:15).
G2194.origine: The name Zebulun comes from the Hebrew זְבוּלוּן (Zəbûlûn), which means "dwelling" or "habitation," evoking the idea of an established home. This name is part of the series of names of Jacob's sons, each carrying a particular significance related to the circumstances of their birth.
G2194.emploi: Zebulun appears three times in the provided New Testament, exclusively in Matthew and Revelation. Matthew mentions him twice in chapter 4, first geographically situating Capernaum within his territory (Matthew 4:13), then citing a prophecy from Isaiah that announces the coming of the Messiah in "the land of Zebulun and Naphtali" (Matthew 4:15). Revelation refers to him during the vision of the sealing of the tribes, counting twelve thousand members of the tribe of Zebulun among the elect (Revelation 7:8). These references show that Zebulun retains its territorial and tribal identity until the end of times.
G2194.portee: Zebulun reminds us that Jesus established His ministry in a region rich in tribal and prophetic history. The choice of Capernaum as the center of His activity in Galilee fulfills ancient promises and demonstrates how God accomplishes His plan of salvation in the concrete history of Israel. The mention of Zebulun in Revelation assures that the Lord does not forget the descendants of the tribes, and that the hope of salvation extends to all the peoples of Israel.

sens: A wealthy tax collector from Jericho
A man of short stature
A man transformed by his encounter with Jesus
G2195.detail: 1. Zacchaeus is a chief tax collector, meaning a supervisor of tax collection in Jericho (Luke 19:2). This was a despised profession among the Jews, who viewed tax collectors as traitors working for Rome and profiting at the expense of their fellow countrymen. 2. Luke emphasizes that Zacchaeus was of short stature (Luke 19:3 states this explicitly in the account). Therefore, he had to climb a sycamore tree to see Jesus pass by: his physical condition prevented him from seeing over the crowd. 3. The encounter with Jesus transforms Zacchaeus: he promises to give half of his possessions to the poor and to repay fourfold anyone he has wronged (Luke 19:8). Jesus then declares that salvation has come to his house, demonstrating the radical change that has taken place in him.
G2195.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew Zakkay, which means "pure" or "innocent." This name stands in stark contrast to the reputation of tax collectors, who were known to be dishonest. Despite his promising name, Zacchaeus had enriched himself in dubious ways before his conversion.
G2195.emploi: Zacchaeus appears only three times in the New Testament, solely in the Gospel of Luke (19:2, 5, 8). Luke presents him as a classic example of Jesus' mercy toward sinners and the marginalized: although wealthy and a tax collector, Zacchaeus is welcomed by Jesus and finds salvation. His story shows how Jesus despises no one and how a true encounter with Him produces authentic repentance and a concrete change of life.
G2195.portee: The story of Zacchaeus teaches that no one is too far from the grace of Jesus, neither too rich nor too compromised. It also shows that true conversion is expressed through concrete actions: Zacchaeus does not settle for good intentions but restores and gives generously. For the believer, Zacchaeus reminds us that Jesus actively seeks those who are lost and that His presence radically transforms those who welcome Him.

sens: Son of Judah and Tamar, ancestor of Jesus
G2196.detail: Zerah is the twin brother of Perez, born of Judah and Tamar. Although the name Zerah means "he who shines" or "rising" (like the sun), he is primarily known because he appears in the genealogy of Jesus recorded by Matthew. This is a remarkable example: Tamar, unable to have children by Judah's sons according to custom, disguised herself to obtain justice, and from this unexpected union, the twins Perez and Zerah were born. Matthew 1:3 mentions Zerah in the lineage of Jesus, showing how God accomplishes His plan of salvation even through unexpected human circumstances.
G2196.origine: The name Zerah comes from the Hebrew זֶרַח (Zérah), which literally means "he who shines" or "rising" (of the sun). This name evokes the image of light appearing, an image of clarity and manifestation. The same Hebrew root is found in other biblical names and expresses the idea of shining or rising.
G2196.emploi: Zerah appears only once in Matthew 1:3, in the genealogy of Jesus presented by Matthew. He is named as the son of Judah, alongside his twin brother Perez. This genealogy traces from Jesus back to Abraham and shows how God has preserved the messianic lineage through generations, despite the difficulties and unusual circumstances surrounding Zerah's birth. His inclusion in this genealogy underscores the importance of his descent in God's divine plan of salvation.
G2196.portee: The mention of Zerah in the genealogy of Jesus reminds us that God does not reject those born of difficult or unexpected circumstances. His story, that of his parents Judah and Tamar, and his place in the family tree of Christ testify to God's grace and faithfulness toward those who seek to live according to His will, even when everything seems compromised.

sens: Father of John the Baptist, priest of God in Judea during the time of Herod
Prophet and priest whose innocent blood was shed between the temple and the altar
G2197G.detail: 1. Zechariah is a faithful and righteous priest who served in the temple of Jerusalem during the reign of King Herod. He is the father of John the Baptist, the forerunner of Jesus. He and his wife Elizabeth had been waiting for a child for a long time when the angel Gabriel announced to him the birth of John. Although initially unbelieving, Zechariah is filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesies about his son's future (Luke 1). 2. Zechariah is also the name of a prophet and priest whose unjust murder Jesus mentions: killed between the altar and the temple in Jerusalem, his innocent blood represents for Jesus the pinnacle of human violence against God's messengers. Jesus says that this generation will have to account for it (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51).
G2197G.origine: The name Zechariah comes from the Hebrew זַכַּי (Zakkaï), which means "God remembers" or "may God remember." It is a name borne by several figures in the history of Israel, notably the prophet Zechariah son of Barachiah during the time of Zerubbabel. The name expresses the confidence that God does not forget His people and remembers His promises.
G2197G.emploi: In the Greek of the New Testament, two characters bear this name. The first is the father of John the Baptist, mentioned in the account of Luke (1:5-67) where he receives the announcement of his son's birth and becomes mute until John's circumcision. The second is a priest and prophet from the Old Testament, whose violent murder is recalled by Jesus as committed by the people of Jerusalem (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51). This second Zechariah, son of Jehoiada (not Barachiah as mistakenly indicated in some manuscripts), represents the persecuted prophets whose blood cries out for vengeance.
G2197G.portee: Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, shows God's faithfulness to those who serve Him with righteousness, even when hope seems lost. His punished unbelief and subsequent conversion teach that God acts despite our doubts. The second Zechariah, whose innocent blood was shed, reminds us that God sees and records every act of injustice, and that He will hold people accountable for it. These two figures invite the believer to trust in divine faithfulness and to have a respectful fear of the One who sees all.

sens: Father of John the Baptist, priest during the time of Herod
Prophet of the Old Testament, son of Jehoiada
G2197H.detail:
1. Zacharias is a Jewish priest from the first century, living during the reign of King Herod. He is married to Elizabeth, who is also of priestly descent. The angel Gabriel announces to him the birth of his son John, who will become the forerunner of Jesus. Doubting this promise, Zacharias is struck mute until the birth of the child (Luke 1:5-22). After naming his son, his mouth is opened and he prophesies about the coming of the Messiah (Luke 1:67-79).
2. Zacharias is also the name of a prophet from the Old Testament, son of the priest Jehoiada, who was stoned by the people for opposing idolatry (Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51 mention him as the last martyr in sacred history before Jesus).
G2197H.origine: The Greek name Zacharias comes from the Hebrew Zakaria (זַכַּי), which literally means "God remembers" or "God remembers favorably." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, borne by several individuals in biblical history. The name reflects trust in God's faithfulness to His people.
G2197H.emploi: The word Zacharias refers to two distinct characters in the New Testament. The father of John the Baptist appears nine times in the Gospel of Luke (chapters 1 and 3), particularly during the account of the Annunciation and the birth of John. The prophet from the Old Testament is mentioned twice by Jesus (Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51) when he laments the rejection of prophets by Jerusalem. These two usages illustrate how the name "Zacharias" transcends the ages: from the little-known prophet of the past to the faithful servant of God who sees the messianic promise fulfilled.
G2197H.portee: The life of Zacharias, the father of John the Baptist, teaches how God honors faithfulness and patient prayer: after a long life of priestly obedience, he receives the grace of being the father of a great prophet. His disbelief, punished and then forgiven, reminds us that even the righteous can doubt, and that God completes our faith with His power. His final praise (the Benedictus) celebrates the irruption of salvation into history: it is the experience of the Christian who discovers how God keeps His promises.

sens: To be alive, to have life (opposed to death)
To lead an existence, to spend one's life in a certain way
To subsist, to nourish oneself
To have a spiritual life, to live by faith
To be active, to function (for a thing)
G2198.detail:
1. To live primarily means to be alive, to breathe, and to physically exist — it is the opposite of being dead. When the centurion's child is healed, his servants say: "Your child lives" (John 4:51), meaning he has regained life. Similarly, Paul states that it is "a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God" (Hebrews 10:31), using the word to refer to God who has life in Himself eternally.
2. To live can also mean to lead a certain form of existence, to have a lifestyle. Thus, Paul says he has "lived as a Pharisee, according to the strictest sect" (Acts 26:5): he speaks of how he spent his life, his habits, and his convictions. It is the idea of living in a particular manner — soberly or foolishly, justly or unjustly.
3. To live can mean to subsist, to nourish oneself to maintain life. Jesus says: "Man shall not live by bread alone" (Matthew 4:4), meaning he needs not only physical food but also the word of God to truly subsist.
4. In the Christian faith, to live takes on a spiritual meaning: it is to welcome Christ into one's heart, to believe in Him and let Him live in us. Paul says: "I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me" (Galatians 2:20). It is a new life, freed from sin, oriented towards God.
5. Sometimes the word applies to things to express that they are active or alive: "living water" (John 4:10) is water that springs from a source, in motion, full of freshness — which spiritually symbolizes the life that God gives.
G2198.origine: The Greek word zaō comes from a root that fundamentally means "to have breath," "to have life." In Hebrew, it translates the word ḥay (חַי), which has the same idea: to be alive, to have breath and life. The phrase "living God" (El ḥay in Hebrew) is a common expression in the Old Testament to express that the true God is the eternal source of life. In Greek, the word zaō forms a family with other words that speak of life: biós (life as duration, lifestyle), psyché (soul, breath of life), zōé (life as vital principle, especially eternal life).
G2198.emploi: The word to live appears about 127 times in the New Testament, in almost all the books. It is first used in the literal sense: someone is alive or dead (1 Corinthians 7:39: "as long as her husband lives"). It then becomes a key word for speaking about moral and religious life: how one "lives" — soberly or foolishly (Luke 15:13), by faith (Galatians 2:20), through righteousness (Romans 6:10-11), by the Spirit (Galatians 5:25). Particularly in Paul, it expresses the new life in Christ: no longer living for oneself, but for the Lord (Romans 14:7-8). John often uses "to live" for the eternal life given by Christ: "He who believes in me will live, even if he dies" (John 11:25-26), where the meaning becomes distinctly spiritual and eternal.
G2198.portee: Understanding this word invites us to ask a central question: how am I truly alive? The Bible does not reduce life to physical breathing; it speaks of true life — one where Christ is at the center, where we walk in righteousness and faith. To live spiritually means to let Christ reign in us, to obey God rather than sin. This word urges the Christian not just to "exist," but to question the quality of their life: am I truly alive for God?

sens: Father of James and John, two of Jesus' twelve apostles
Fisherman in Galilee who owned a boat
Man whose family was called to follow Jesus
G2199G.detail:
1. Zebedee is a man from Galilee, the father of two sons who become apostles: James and John (Matthew 4:21). These two brothers work as fishermen with their father.
2. He owns a boat and a net repair shop on the lake (Matthew 4:21; Mark 1:19). He is a man of some means, not just a hired hand.
3. His wife asks Jesus for a place of honor for her two sons in the Kingdom (Matthew 20:20), showing that the family is close to Jesus and believes in Him. Peter and the two sons of Zebedee are also among those who accompany Jesus in His moments of trial (Matthew 26:37).
G2199G.origine: The Hebrew name Zəbadyāh (Heb. זְבַדְיָה) literally means "God has given" or "gift of the Lord" (from zabad = to give and yah = God). This name was common in Israel. In the Septuagint, it is rendered by various forms: Zβδαδαῖος, Zβδειά, reflecting variations in the transcription of the Hebrew name into Greek.
G2199G.emploi: Zebedee appears eleven times in the Gospels, exclusively in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. He is mentioned primarily as "the father of James and John," which shows that his importance in the Gospel narrative entirely depends on the fact that his sons are called by Jesus. He is encountered three times acting concretely: fishing with his sons (Matthew 4:21; Mark 1:19), during Jesus' calling. The mother of his sons plays a more visible role in the story (Matthew 20:20), while Zebedee himself fades into the background after the calling. He symbolizes the link of the earthly family with the new faith.
G2199G.portee: Zebedee reminds us that Jesus' call transcends family ties without destroying them. His sons left the boat, nets, and father to follow the Master, responding to a greater call. However, their connection to Zebedee does not disappear: he is remembered, honored by recalling who he was. It is a lesson on the priority of the Kingdom while respecting one's origins.
